title: New Kickstarter for Wyldwood from Tabletop Titans Live
content:
Today marks the beginning of the Kickstarter Campaign for Wyldwood, brought to life by Tabletop Titans, following their previous two successful campaigns. We had a chance to take a look at the game during UK Games Expo, and had to admit the huge models were impressive on the table -- Rurik below is on a 120mm base. Tabletop Titans hopes to bring Wyldwood to your homes and LGS near you, with the campaign promising retail and organized play following the release of the game.

Rurik. Credit: Tabletop Titans

So far everything about Wyldwood looks great, and we'll be taking a closer, sponsored look at the game as the campaign progresses. Tabletop Titans promises an easy to pick up and play game and hopes that the larger models with low overall count can help make it an excellent first stop for new players, as well as providing some painting challenge and inspiration for others! If you'd like to check out the campaign and possibly support it yourself, you can do so through the link here.

title: Games Industry News Roundup- September 15th, 2026
content:
Here at Tabletop Battles, we know that it’s hard to keep track of all the news happening all the time in the games industry. So much is always going on, all over the place, all the time. With games of all sorts, and their related media, being an informed gamer can feel impossible some days. 

That's why every week, we help you stay in the know by rounding up five of the biggest recent stories in the gaming and gaming-related pop culture sphere in the Games Industry News Roundup. Our trusty news boy, Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson, is right here at the very real, and cool TTB newsdesk with the scoop.

Credit: Card Kingdom

Card Kingdom Pending Acquisition by ZMC Subsidiary

One of our frequent Magic: The Gathering writers, Saffgor, joins us this week to discuss the bombshell news of Card Kingdom’s potential acquisition that flew under the radar in August.

Saffgor: Private Equity is lengthening the shadow it casts on the TCG space, with Strauss Zelnick's PE firm ZMC now announced to purchase a majority stake in Card Kingdom, the second-largest online purchasing platform for Magic: The Gathering.

This is weird on several levels, because the headline you've likely read is something like "CK purchased by Citadel LLC", which is misleading in a few ways. The Citadel purchasing Card Kingdom isn't the same Citadel involved in the $GME nonsense, but instead an acquisition LLC formed for this purchase by ZMC as a means to isolate liabilities. In addition, the announcement of this sale was made via the UFCW3000 union website on August 17th. The story's only broken into the mainstream because of a Reddit post of the link by someone who frequents r/mtgfinance, and mentions of it from employees on Twitter or Bluesky are nonexistent.

Why all of this matters comes down to the fact that not only is CK the second-largest online retailer for the biggest TCG, but that they manage physical locations via Mox Boarding House, and have an active union. Their main competitor, TCGPlayer, was accused of engaging in union-busting activities following their acquisition by eBay in 2022/23, and while Card Kingdom has made a public statement that all union employees will be retained at current wages & benefit status, at time of writing the union itself has *not* met with Citadel Acquisition, nor their parent ZMC.

ZMC's history with unions has been an unpleasant one, as you might expect from private equity. In 2025, Second City's employees threatened a strike backed by the Actor's Equity Association, following a lack of pay rise after ZMC's direct acquisition of the company in 2021, and managed to bargain for a salary increase of up to 40% over a five-year period. Rockstar (parent company Take-Two being managed by ZMC)1) meanwhile is embroiled in its own allegations of union busting by former employees with hearings expected to run through October. The plaintiffs are 34 employees, and their termination followed closely behind the 10% membership required for union recognition (in the UK) at the Glasgow office.

Until the acquisition is finalized, reported to occur in late September, we won't know further details without public filings or internal leaks.

IGN Hit with New Round of Layoffs

Credit: IGN

IGN, the largest source for games related news on the web, is going through another round of layoffs at all levels, including two of its longtime video content hosts. 

According to a report from Kotaku and various posts from former employees, IGN underwent a sweeping round of layoffs across multiple departments. As of this writing, IGN hasn’t released any sort of statement acknowledging the layoffs, so the exact number of people affected remains unclear, but a few notable faces at IGN were confirmed as let go in social media posts. Some of those staff members were highly visible longtime video content hosts, including Seth Macy from the Nintendo Voice Chat podcast and Brian Altano from Playstation Beyond.

Bo Moore, senior manager of tech coverage, wrote on their social media about being let go from IGN. “My team had a huge content day today on IGN, covering the launch of Valve’s Steam Frame. So this seems like a good time as any to say that I was affected by today’s layoffs. My byline is only on one of the 7 stories we posted this morning, but I edited every one, worked late last week and logged on early this morning to make sure everything was on track for one of our biggest coverage days of the year.”

Aftermath later reported that the IGN Creators Guild, the union representing many of the team members at IGN, were not given advance warning of the layoffs, as leadership had done in the past, leaving union leadership in the dark on who was let go. The Creators Guild would release a statement on Bluesky later the same day expressing their anger and disappointment.

"Today was an awful day at IGN. We were blindsided by the layoff of four union members and many more people across the organization who contributed years of their careers to making IGN an unparalleled voice in games and entertainment.

"With each successive layoff, core parts of IGN's operation continue to be stripped away. Today, IGN has decided to do away with many of our talented producers, editors, hosts, and other crucial roles, both within and out of the union. How many layoffs will occur before we no longer recognize the company we work for and the content that we make?

"While we recognize the challenges the media industry is facing as a whole, it is difficult to understand how laying off valuable employees better positions us to meet those challenges. In turn, remaining employees bear additional workloads worsened by anxiety over the ever-looming threat of another layoff.

"We are devastated, angry, and heartbroken for our colleagues."

This round of layoffs at the gaming journalism giant is the largest since the mass layoffs at IGN last summer, which culminated in IGN’s publisher, John Davison, walking away from the site. He has not been formally replaced.

UK’s Biggest Saga Retailer Closes Its Doors

Credit: Gripping Beast

The inexorable march of time waits for no one, grinding down everything in its path in the slow, relentless turn of its wheels. In this case, “no one” includes one of the largest retailers for historical miniatures in the UK, Gripping Beast. In a post on their social media page, the company announced that they would be shutting down their operations in the near future, as after thirty years of operations and multiple team member retirements they simply can no longer sustainably run operations. 

“Gripping Beast has been around since 1996, and it's been quite a journey,” the team writes. “Over the years, we've built up a collection of more than 6,000 historical and fantasy miniatures, while also taking on Front Rank and Lurkio and continuing to run their ranges alongside our own. We've also had the pleasure of supporting guest ranges from Calpe Miniatures and Ragnarok Miniatures and many others.

“Most importantly, we've had the support of thousands of fantastic customers over the years. Many of them have become friends and fellow gamers, and we've been lucky enough to meet and share the hobby with people from all over the world. Their enthusiasm and support have been a huge part of our journey, and we're incredibly grateful for it.

“Sadly, the time has come for us to admit that we unfortunately aren’t getting any younger, some of us are getting considerably creakier, and our small team has been reduced by recent retirements. So, after a lot of thought (and not enough tea), we have decided that it is time for us to close the doors at Beast Towers.”

The team at Gripping Beast intends to close up shop slowly, rather than all at once, continuing their operations and keeping the online store up for the time being. Gripping Beast does note that as it begins to wind down though, the online store will be shut down, at which point the team will focus on fulfilling the remaining orders before shutting down for good. 

In a follow up post, Gripping Beast clarifies this timeline, saying, “Months rather than weeks but we really can't say for certain and don't want to make promises we can't keep. Bare in mind [sic] the retirement is largely due to  ongoing health issues and health can be very unpredictable.”

The product lines that Gripping Beast produces, but does not own, will have manufacturing rights returned to the original game designers once Gripping beast closes. As for SAGA, the largest miniature line produced by Gripping Beast, the company notes that “North Star Military Figures have taken on SAGA distribution already, Studio Tomahawk make and produce this game still and will continue to do so.”

Gripping Beast does note that they would be open to an interested buyer purchasing the company and taking over operations for themselves, and welcomes any serious offers to reach out to them to discuss. 

Credit: Blizzard Entertainment

Blizzard Ratifies Historic Union Agreement 

In a spot of unabashed good news in the video game industry, after two years of negotiations employees across all sectors of Blizzard Entertainment successfully ratified a union contract with leadership, covering around 1900 employees with various labor rights, AI protections, and protections against layoffs.

Bargaining committee member and Principal Software Engineer Daniel Weltz told the Communications Workers of America “I’ve been at Blizzard for 20 years because I love this company and the amazing people I work with. This contract secures a lot of what people already love about working here while adding strong protections around layoffs, job security, and remote work. Blizzard helped shape the gaming industry, and I’m proud that this contract allows us to continue setting new standards for this work.”

The negotiations initially began with the different unionized development teams within Blizzard in 2024, but since their initial formation little headway had been made between leadership and the unionized workers. While workers organizing and making their voices heard was certainly effective in getting leadership attention, that wasn’t what finally got things really moving with the bargaining. According to a recent interview from Aftermath however, Union negotiators were able to bring Microsoft leadership around by pointing out how much easier and effective it would be to negotiate for all of the development teams and departments at once, rather than a contract for each individual entity. Thus, the primary negotiators on the World of Warcraft team eventually evolved into negotiating for the entire company, with other leaders from each department contributing.

The final contract secured multiple big protections for Blizzard workers, which are vital as Microsoft is still in the middle of its year-long restructuring efforts with 1,600 more employees still scheduled for some form of layoff. These concessions from leadership include strong layoff protections and severance packages, as well as 14 month recall rights should any position open up at Blizzard that a laid off employee would be qualified for. Negotiators also managed to secure better pay for Blizzard employees, as well as job security against AI and remote work protections.

“CWA members at Blizzard are leading the way for all XBOX studios, showing what can be achieved when video game workers have a strong voice in shaping their studios for the better,” writes Claude Cummings Jr, president of the CWA. “It’s a new day at Blizzard, where greater power for workers is translating into more innovative games for players. I am so proud of CWA bargaining teams, taking on tough fights and winning strong contracts that set new standards for working people across our industries.” 

Credit: Steve Jackson Games

Steve Jackson Stepping Down as CEO of Steve Jackson Games

Oh hey, it's our good buddy time again. Back so soon, wow! Who are you crushing under those slow and relentless wheels of yours this time? Steve Jackson, you say? Wait, which one? Oh, gotcha, the American, cool cool cool. 

Yes, Steve Jackson, creator of GURPS and Munchkin and founder Steve Jackson games (not to be confused with Steve Jackson, co-founder of Games Workshop), is retiring from his role as CEO at his company to step into a games designer role, passing the torch of CEO to longtime employee Sabrina Gonzalez.

Jackson founded Steve Jackson games in 1980, and has since then become one of the most prolific tabletop games designers in America. His most notable works, like GURPS, Ogre, Munchkin, and Zombie Dice, have earned him international critical acclaim and commercial popularity. 

After over forty years at the helm, Jackson is passing the torch to Sabrina Gonzalez, who joined the company in 2013. While at Steve Jackson Games, she's worked in several roles, including Production Artist and Production Manager, as well as serving on the company Board since 2021. Additionally, Gonzalez briefly stepped away from Steve Jackson Games to work on the manufacturing side of the games industry, which gives her additional insight that will be invaluable in her new role.

“As a general goal, I'd like us to continue to grow,” Gonzalez wrote in the announcement. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request."

Alongside Gonzalez’s promotion, Managing Editor Allison Page is stepping into the role of Chief Operating Officer at Steve Jackson Games. Page has been with the company since 2023, and is looking forward to her new position alongside Gonzalez.

"I'm most excited to support Sabrina in her new role as CEO!” Page writes. “We've always worked really well together and want the same things for SJ Games. I'm a problem solver, and I'm passionate about setting clear expectations. I'm excited to untangle whatever comes my way and ensure the team knows how to move forward and has what they need."

While the post does state that Steve Jackson, the man, is staying on to help design games at Steve Jackson Games, the company, it is unclear if he will do so in a full time capacity or if he intends to step back into more of an advisory role within the design team.

title: MTG Reality Fracture reveals a green version of blue's most busted enchantment
content:
Long-time MtG fans are being spoiled by the card reveals for Reality Fracture. The mirror 'echoverse' conceit has let the designers cut loose, packing the set with deep cut references to iconic cards, each one with a witty color-shifted twist. I've picked out three of the most remarkable cards from the latest batch of spoilers that you need to look out for.

Omnipresence is a green mirror to Omniscience, the iconic enchantment that allows you to cast spells for free. Revealed on Screen Rant on Monday, this hefty mythic costs three green and five generic mana, making it two pips cheaper than Omniscience - but since most Omniscience strategies try to cheat the pivotal enchantment into play, that discount isn't very relevant.

Omnipresence is far more constricted, since it only allows you to cast spells for free if their mana value is less than or equal to the number of creatures you control. The fact Omnipresence doesn't provide any kind of mana advantage unless you have creatures in play means it's nowhere near the power level of Omniscience, a card that can win you the game from one life point and an empty board if you have the right hand.

Still, monogreen Commander decks aren't short of ramp, creature tokens, and spells that cost a lot of mana, and there will be board states where this will let you cast your entire deck. It'll find a home.

Two MTG cards, Entrust the Spark and Natural OrderDraconic Visitor is a red reimagining of Divine Visitation, the white enchantment that turns all creature tokens you create into angels. This really feels like a perfect translation of that design from white to red. Instead of an enchantment, Draconic Visitor is a 5/5 flying dragon; instead of turning creature tokens into angels it turns artifact tokens into yet more 5/5 flying dragons. All that for just two red and three generic mana.

This is going to be a limited bomb, and in Commander it's frankly hilarious. Obviously it has a home in dragon decks, and Redditors have already spotted that it goes infinite with Ganax, a dragon commander from Battle for Baldur's Gate who creates a treasure token every time a dragon enters under your control. On its own that loop will just draw the game, but you can turn it into a win with a Terror of the Peaks, Scourge of Valkas, Impact Tremors, Goblin Bombardment, or any number of other red spells.

Variety got to reveal a few cards on Tuesday, and by far the most interesting is Entrust the Spark. In mechanical terms this is 'Natural Order' for planeswalkers. For one green, one blue, and three colorless mana, this sorcery lets you sacrifice a planeswalker - probably one of the new Jace tokens from this set - to search up another Planeswalker from your deck and put it into play.

Super Friends players are going to love this card. Think of it as a wildcard that will let you replace whichever Planeswalker is closest to death with whichever you need the most (and failing that, whichever costs the most). Over in Standard, spending five mana to turn a Jace token into Ugin, Eye of the Storms seems pretty appealing.

Reality Fracture is shaping up to be one of the coolest MTG sets in months, if not years. Which echoverse cards are you most excited to play with? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: In the Land of the Sundering Flood
content:
For various virtually unbelievable reasons, I’ve been spending a lot of time walking in the footsteps of William Morris, the great artist, craftsperson, visionary and theorist of the arts and crafts movement*. Morris has inspired my work in the hobby for a long time, but often forgotten is his foundational inspiration of what we now call fantasy, largely through his posthumously published novel The Sundering Flood.

*to the extent all photos in this article are of Mammoth Miniatures models photographed in the grounds of the William Morris Museum.

The Sundering Flood is one of the first fantasy novels as we’d now understand it, a foundational work that caught the imagination of Tolkien and all that followed. If it’s the grandfather of modern fantasy, it’s also the ancestor of everything we do here, the wellspring of a lineage that sees us deluged in plastic and metal to this day. Acknowledging and honouring that debt is a hard task, but after a successful Kickstarter in 2025, Nic Evans of Mammoth Miniatures has shown he’s more than up to it, with a fantastic melding of miniature gameplay, Morris’ fantasy and the philosophy of the arts and crafts movement.

That’s the big man’s house in the background In The Land of the Sundering Flood. From Mammoth Miniatures. Credit: lenoon

In the Land of the Sundering Flood takes the form of a small (in all ways) rulebook describing a character driven skirmish game, that focuses as much time and page count on the work of William Morris as it does the core rules. It’s a great example of one of my favourite things in modern miniature gaming, where a designer takes an idea, a theme, even a philosophy, and tries earnestly to translate everything about it into a gaming experience. I think it’s done admirably here, and strongly recommend picking up In the Land of the Sundering Flood as a result.

Gameplay

In the meat of it, this is a skirmish level game where a good sized force will include 4-10 models. It’s a granular and individual model driven game (no squad rules here!), where each model will have its own kit, rules and actions to take. Dice rolls are skill checks, with each character given a dice pool and target values to hit for successes, often with a corresponding opposed roll. It feels detailed - each model moves and acts independently, equipment lists are short but meaningful and models have limited numbers of actions per turn. The focus is very much on what an individual model can do, supported by careful design that makes everyone feel unique. The raw bones of it would work very well as the entirety of an RPGs combat system, especially one where you’re there to tell stories before you fight.

In The Land of the Sundering Flood. From Mammoth Miniatures. Credit: lenoon

Fighting - what you’re going to use this for - is quite RPG styled. You make a skill check to hit (and defend), and, weapon dependent damage is dealt, effects applied, enemies are pushed back and life pools depleted. It’s satisfyingly clear, with visually defined dice pools and obvious target numbers. Two non-combat themed characters trying to swing fists into each other will feel pretty pillowy - but that’s what range (and weirds) are for. There’s no batch or fast rolling here - a combat is a back and forth of manually rolled dice, where elements form patterns that repeat (the pattern might be a giant squashes a skinner over and over again, but whatever the pattern is, it’s still a pattern). It’s all by hand, with a clean and clear process that’s fast enough to play but not fast enough to make combats a blur of “4s then 3s and 5s to save”. That’s all very Morris-y (not very Morrissey, an entirely different and shitty thing), the gaming equivalent of carefully lifting and placing print blocks or moveable type - deliberate, calculated, on theme but not archaic or laborious.

That’s a good line for all of it really, because for all the retro styling, the gameplay experience is modern and straightforward. There’s very little rerolling and no play by intent, fast rolling is out (nothing makes you roll enough dice to need it), but it’s not a clunky, slow, look-it-up-in-the-rule book play experience. A read through gives you enough to get going, and then scenario play gives you more than enough variety to dig in. Assembling armies is pleasantly loose but not horrifically open to abuse. You can take mighty heroes, but you’re also going to take the guys that tag along with them, who feel neither meaningless nor superpowered. You can (and should! Feels right) hand write your lists out, and games last long enough for collaborative storytelling without feeling like DnD with even more minis.

That’s quite an important point, as in the land of the sundering flood is explicitly “a stand alone knightly combat game or part of a larger narrative adventure game”. It’s written as the combat section of an adventure - terrain is taken as a given to be themed (“it is admirable and joyous to construct a true landscape in which to play”), and provided scenarios give a flavour of different ways you can (should? Must? Are called to?) play the game. The presumption is always that there’s a reason your models are where they are, that they have a job to do (or weird to fulfill), that each game is a slice of time within the land of the flood.

Theming

This is a game clearly written and designed from the ground up with the source material in mind. There’s a lot of games that claim that, but few stick to it. You can certainly play MESBG to the battles of the books and the films, but mechanically it doesn’t reflect how the characters operate in the fiction. Aragorn can (and will) scythe through Uruk Hai, but he lacks a mechanism to make his speech at the gate of the deep. Here though, the base mechanics and the wyrd combine to make this the game of the book (TM) - deliberate, crafted and occasionally magical. Hero characters will mow down opponents until they run into a suitably destined fight, the kind that a chapter might lead up to. The fey manipulate the skein of reality for purposes unknown and unseeable, and their effects are tricksy. This kind of design permeates everything in the book, from the look down to the simplest mechanics. Movement is a good example - characters have compound movement values, a knight will have a speed of L (9cm), while a wily fae could be S+S (10cm). A model can move up to its full movement, or partially, but the sequencing is important. You move the knight once (L), but you must move the fae twice (s+s). It’s a small difference but a subtle one, where a creature that flits across the field and a storming warrior feel different as they move. The player interacts with them in different ways, a materiality of play that lends both thematic and para-ludic meaning to the action. The craftsperson takes deliberate time to move, twice, by hand. All very William Morris, and a testament to the attention to detail put into the game.

In The Land of the Sundering Flood. From Mammoth Miniatures. Credit: lenoon

This carries on beyond the rules, into the look, feel and language of the game. This is, very simply, a gorgeous book. Illustrations are beautiful, a vintage fantasy styling drawn by Nick at Mammoth Miniatures that pulls Morris’ work through the lens of Ian Miller. Character illustrations are exceptional - Mammoth Miniatures always has good form here - with striking and occasionally arresting use of black and white to bring forth evocative resonance of creatures and heroes unknown. Rules and background pages have absolutely gorgeous borders that create a touch of grimdark fantasy to the Morris and Burne-Jones style. Even the text - set in (what else!) Morris and Co type. The amazing thing, really, is that none of this gets in the way of clarity. Rules are presented well, the game is straightforward to understand and stat blocks are gorgeously clear and visually obvious. It’s a hell of a compliment to give, but it looks, feels and plays like something the arts and crafts movement would have come up with. I can see those strange, blessed, visionary men and women sitting in the Red House late of an evening - someone pulls out the board (exquisite, of course), and the dice. Perhaps they talk a little of socialism and hope for the future before the first dice is rolled and the game begins.

It might be a bit of an indulgence, but I think that setting is important. This game is designed to play among friends who are into it, into the whole thing, who will adore the typesetting and the marginalia, and who will ignore the fact that one of the scenarios cuts off the forces so you don’t have a strict points limit. This is a good game, mechanically speaking, but it won’t appeal to everyone. If your hobby is all about systems mastery, shooting angles and being crowned champion of champions, then it isn’t really for you. You might like it, of course, but this is game as story, as art form. It’s a couple of lovingly painted miniatures (hand sculpted, of course!) playing over a meter square of terrain, telling a story of Knightly combat, faerie caprice and sinister villainy. It’s the kind of game where you interrupt your turn to give a speech, or you play as the culmination of a weekend’s collective painting and discussion. It begs to be played in a drawing room by the fire, or in the park in the footsteps of the man himself.

Delving and Spinning

In The Land of the Sundering Flood. From Mammoth Miniatures. Credit: lenoon

Land of the sundering flood is a game that hews close to the source in telling a story through structure and mechanic, a place where the how and why of writing is equal to the output. Fittingly, the rules, models, story and feel of the game is artisan - boutique, but mass producible, overall, handmade. There’s a joy in the handmade and I think there’s something here that speaks to it. I don’t tend to agree with the strict oldhammer position - everything should be sculpted in green stuff and milliput, because I think design can be computer aided in the same way it is aided by brush or pin - but to some extent I do sympathise with it. It is a rejection of the modern; a rejection of the insidious influence of capital, of growth, of the idea that a miniatures company can - and is - somewhere in the FTSE 250. It can hark back to a golden age with all the nostalgic poison of fascism, sometimes, but it can also celebrate a love of the game as opposed to of the release schedule. There’s definitely a good way and a bad way to draw from the past, where we can drown in nostalgia or reinvent through a modern lens - here, mammoth have managed the latter. Land of the sundering flood speaks to the process of capital in the miniatures hobby much as the man himself spoke to it in art and design. It is ok to slow down, to move by hand, to accept the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune without reroll or probability smoothing, to spend your time playing a story that could have come from the prose Edda instead of Abnett. Our luck is that we can look forward, much as Morris did, and take what is good and just about the present and combine it with what is worth remembering about the past, and luckily we have games like Land of the Sundering flood to show us how. We have gained so, so much from the way the modern hobby, its rulesets and models, operates, and we live in a better time for hobbyists that ever before as a result - but games like in the land of the sundering flood remind us not of what we have lost, but what we still have before us. Art, beauty, peace, pleasure. Morris, I feel, would be proud.

title: Thunder Road: Ignition is a shining example of a board game tuning up, and pricing down
content:
Our Verdict

Ignition is an A-Tier gateway game, thanks to rock solid, rapid, replayable, easy, mixed-group gaming, a well executed theme, and a surprisingly good look and feel (given the budget price). Budget priced conversion jobs rarely deliver the same horsepower as their full fat predecessors - but Ignition proves it can be done, and done well.

Pros
  • Keeps the original's tight actions and fast play
  • Design changes from Vendetta are genius
  • Superb presentation and build quality, despite cost cuts
Cons
  • Strategy play is shallow
  • Lacks some of Vendetta's crunch
  • Simple plastic cars sap some immersion

I am, generally speaking, Not A Big Fan of car board games. So, when Restoration Games' team racked up $762,000 on Kickstarter for Thunder Road: Vendetta in 2023, I just watched with interest from the stands, eating an oilstained hot dog and breathing in the gasoline. It's never quite made my shopping list since, either; $60 is hardly expensive, but it's dear enough to disqualify it from being a 'little treat' impulse buy.

Apparently, I'm not alone, because Restoration (more specifically designers Noah Cohen, Rob Daviau, Justin D. Jacobson, and Justin Kemppainen) have specifically engineered the new version, Thunder Road: Ignition, to deliver the same post-apocalyptic, rock-em-sock-em racing for half the cash. And, blow it all, if they haven't done exactly that. Restoration Games kindly handed me a free review copy at Gen Con, and it's been my pleasure to learn that a) I really should have been playing Vendetta all along, and b) I don't need to now - because this game is at least as good.

If you, like me, didn't play Thunder Road: Vendetta, we should cover the basics first (TR:V veterans, feel free to jump straight to the changes in Ignition). Note also that all the images below are of my copy of Ignition - partly because, with a few exceptions and missing helicopters, there's very little, visually, to tell between them. Trust me, it'll make sense.

The baseline: Thunder Road Vendetta

So, Vendetta is our starting point. One of classic game-rebooting specialist Restoration Games' biggest success stories, Brett Myers and Dave Chalker's board game is a reimplementation of designer Jim Keifer's 1986 creation Thunder Road, which was itself, er, 'inspired' by the original Mad Max movie that came out in the US six years before.

You're a desperate, gas mask-clad daredevil in a souped up, gun-armed scrap wagon, and you're racing along a post-apocalyptic American highway with absolutely zero health and safety regulations. You control three cars (one large, one medium, one small), and whoever gets one of theirs across the finish line first is the winner.

The straight road starts with three interlocking sections, but each time a car reaches the end of one, a new stretch is added from a random stack, and the rearmost segment removed from the game, along with any unfortunate drivers still lagging behind there. Only once the second additional tile is added does the finish line come into view at its end.

You can't get there by just being fastest, though; this is a death race. You've got to clear your path to the chequered flag by ramming rivals' cars off the road or into obstacles (called a Slam), and/or using your in-built machine guns to wreck the vehicles in your way. Big cars are better at ramming, but easier to shoot; small ones vice versa.

The action economy is as grinningly unsubtle, yet effective as the theme. Each round, you first roll four six sided dice and reserve them. Each turn, you then apply a die to one of your cars and move that many spaces. The forth die you'll use to trigger a special Command ability, once per round.

You can Repair damage from a car; use Nitro for an extra move; Drift a car to overtake someone without Slamming them; or order an Airstrike, having your pet Helicopter swoop in and shoot a rival.

That's the bones of the game right there - but the meat is in the destructive melee you'll wreak with those tools, as the inevitable circus of collisions causes cascading chaos.

Almost everything on the track is there to ensure the cars smash into each other as often as possible. Even if every player's on a pacifist run, terrain obstacles scattered along the track ensure the Destruction Derby doesn't become a Regular Derby.

Oil slicks send you skidding into other cars. Impassable rockslides are instant death to any unlucky enough to career into them. Landmines will blow half your car off if you roll over one.

Take damage twice, and your car becomes inoperable until Repaired - but stays on the road in the meantime, as an obstacle that'll trigger further Slams when driven into.

And here's the kicker: Slams beget Slams. Hit another car, and you'll stack your car on top of the other one before rolling two neat, custom 'FX' dice. One tells you which car (top or bottom) gets shunted, and the other shows you which adjacent space they're shunted into. If said shunted-into space also contains a car, another Slam begins, with no limit to how many can be triggered this way. It's Slams all the way down, baby - and these cascading wreck scenarios are, unsurprisingly, some of the game's funniest and best moments.

So, that's the original game, Vendetta. It's a big $60 box with multi part, multi color plastic cars and cute little choppers with rotating rotors. Ignition costs just a tad over half that much, aiming to "streamline play for an easier and quicker point-of-entry". So, what got cut, and what's left?

What's changed in Ignition?

Describing Vendetta's gameplay in detail right up top was a very deliberate choice for this Ignition review, because - spoilers - almost everything is exactly the same.

The cheaper version has fewer moving parts than the 2023 original - both metaphorically and physically. But, as the incomparable Dan Thurot rightly says in his Space Biff review, this really only serves to amplify Thunder Road's greatest strengths (momentum and slapstick mayhem), to the point where it's arguably superior to its more expensive older sibling.

Let's examine the change notes. First up, no more choppers. That's a quarter of the plastic minis eliminated, right away. We trade the tactility of playing with a chopper toy for the Missile action, which shoots an imaginary rocket at a rival car instead, but otherwise works exactly the same.

Second, the toy cars are worse. Instead of each vehicle being multiple different colored injection molded parts fitted together, like a proper toy, Ignition's are hollow, one piece, single injection jobs. They're still cute, they're still detailed, it still feels good to stack 'em - but they look and feel cheap, because they are.

Third, cars can't die now. There's no Repair action for damaged cars, no inoperable cars staying on the board, and no eliminations either; if your car crashes or takes two damage, it just goes off for a pit stop and comes back next turn, at a predetermined re-entry point that's usually several spaces behind its grave site. The trade-off is that it then misses a go, unless you spend your one Command for that round to bring it back on immediately (that Jumpstart action replaces Repair on the Command Board).

And forth, on a related note: instead of a straight road that randomly generates new sections during the game, Ignition has the complete track laid out from the get-go, it's shorter, and it now has bends in it. As far as I can tell, the kinks in the road have little effect on the gameplay, but they're a small change that, for me, boosts the game's atmos. And, crucially, the shorter track (combined with other streamlining) cuts play time from 45-75 minutes down to 25-45.

Though I haven't played Vendetta, these two feel like the biggest changes here. There are fewer states for a car to be in, with less friction between them; things move more smoothly; and the competition stays tighter from start to finish, because no team gets left behind or knocked out of the running. The slight balancer is that you now have to get two cars over the line to win, rather than just one.

On the other hand, no car death means there's no option to win through vehicular murder alone, and it also means no mangled car wrecks adding dynamic new obstacles to the track, so those have just been removed from the box. Another saving on plastic, but perhaps a bit of life, death, and thrill sucked out too. Your mileage may vary.

Priced down, tuned up?

I'll be honest, I went into testing Thunder Road: Ignition with only a passing knowledge of the original Vendetta, and only while doing wider research for this review did I discover how similar the two games are.

Considering the specific, streamlining amendments by Restoration's designers added a much needed layer of context to the (already very positive) initial opinions I had from my test games. As a result I was left  even more impressed with Ignition, not just as a cut-price adaptation but as a game in its own right.

Just from playing it, Ignition defeated my anti-car prejudices and slammed its way into my gateway game rotation, right alongside fellow newcomer Magical Athlete and my beloved Azul. Just from opening the box, it was clear Ignition had somehow kept most of its big sister's aesthetic quality intact despite a 42% price reduction - an unusual achievement in itself.

But doing all that with gameplay adaptations that, at worst, achieve a slightly different thing just as well and, at best, achieve the same thing, better, for less money, is what elevates Ignition from 'great' to 'exceptional'.

For a lot of existing Vendetta fans, this isn't going to be a necessary play. If you already love the bigger game, you might miss your choppers, the random extra track tiles, or the thrill of winning mostly by murdering your enemies. And sure, the cars feel cheap, because they are cheap. But sometimes, cheap games can feel like a million bucks - and this one does.

If you're itching to tell me why I'm wrong and the bendy roads change EVERYTHING, or why I've utterly missed the point because I haven't played Vendetta, come park your scrap wagon in the free Wargamer Discord community and tell me so! I'd genuinely love to learn more, and hey, stick around for the constant, unhinged tabletop chats, giveaways, AMAs, and more!

title: Magic: The Gathering Puzzlebox – Empower Jace with a New 2-Card Combo
content:
The role of Planeswalkers in Magic have charted a course towards normalcy, even banality, in their 19 years of existence. First debuting in Lorwyn, this was a card type whispered about with excitement since their first teaser on Tarmogoyf, with each adding to the others’ mythos. Here was one of the most powerful Creatures printed in years, mentioning with blasé that yes, the most powerful characters in the game’s history would soon be playable in your deck, not just in the pages of the game’s novels. We take for granted how utterly cool this all was, yet as the years have gone by, the narrative of Planeswalkers as a game piece has been that of an albatross around the designers’ necks. Essentially all Universes Beyond sets decline to include them, as Magic is the only story to contain the concept at its most literal, and the most popular format is hostile to their play—with three opponents, and being locked to once per turn cycle, Commander isn’t a happy home for most Planeswalkers. Yet, in spite of this changing landscape, Magic’s second real Planeswalkers-matter set is dropping this fall, and in Reality Fracture, a new innovation is emerging: Planeswalker tokens. Heck, OG Tarmogoyf is even back in Standard! Does this crossroads of past and future fix the issue of the card type, or make it all the more mundane? Let’s talk about getting the most out of Empowering Jace.

This is part of a shortform Magic series where I’m covering rapid-fire concepts about Commander that I couldn’t cover in a full Commander Focus, so if you like what you see, certainly let us know!

Planeswalk the Walk

Fittingly, Empower Jace X is akin to Amass X, being a spin on a mechanic introduced originally in the first Planeswalkers-matter set, War of the Spark. If you lack a token Jace, first you create one: A non-Legendary Blue Planeswalker with no mana cost, and no means of innately increasing his own Loyalty. Then, however many Loyalty counters noted on the Empower are placed on a token Jace you control. Like with Amass, any means of doubling the number of tokens you create will still require you place the noted number of Loyalty counters on just one, meaning the other immediately dies, but in a similar vein, ways of duplicating the trigger or number of counters do indeed work to grow Jace’s loyalty to outrageous levels. While innately this means you just get a fancy Phyrexian Arena, there’s a host of cards which afford new abilities to Planeswalkers, and more arriving this set. Two early standouts are ">Ichormoon Gauntlet (whose price has already skyrocketed) and Kasmina, Enigma Sage...who is actually the better of the two, funny enough. If you resolve a Jace’s Machinations with her onboard, congratulations on the Instant-speed Enter the Infinite (or whatever big Blue spell, really).

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Pending additional spoilers, the other option at time of writing is Rewrite the Multiverse with 8+ Creatures onboard, which is a bit more expensive, but better on its own. Kasmina herself is fairly easy to find, and tutoring for a 3 mana Blue Instant is even easier, so this package is definitely in the cards for a competitive list. It’s a compelling 2-card combo, even if the addition of other colors makes finding pieces all that much simpler, on top of redundancy for other means of Empowering Jace 8+ in a single instance. If you’re willing to set up an engine, however, Avatar of Burgeoning Echoes can probably get a Jace with the necessary loyalty over the course of a few turns, and is already in the same colors as Kasmina. If you play Land ramp, going from a fetch into two drops in one turn with the Avatar already onboard isn’t out of the question. The early frontrunner for Kasmina lines is, in my eyes, The Eighth Doctor+Susan Foreman, with resilience via 8th, and Susan providing early mana and a body with which to do Birthing Pod/Eldritch Evolution lines via Academy Rector. Plus, with Susan being your ramp on 2, you can jam a comical number of 4-mana ramp spells which find 2 Lands, in turn helping to make Avatar a better means of hitting our critical 8 loyalty.

The Jace-stice League

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Going one by one, let’s start with my favorite sub-archetype in Commander: Scramble. Named after Reality Scramble, this set of ~3 cards (also including Chaotic Transformation & Reweave) turns one permanent into another random one of its shared type, directly from your Library. This is the first time we’ve had access to token Planeswalkers, though, so while Scramble has existed for Commanders like Jeska, Thrice Reborn & Dihada, Binder of Wills, never before have you been able to do it outside of the Command Zone. If you Empower Jace (available in all five colors, and Colorless), that gives you the capacity to flip it into another Planeswalker of your choice, with reduced room for countermagic. If you’re all-in on Empower Jace, this can just be Kasmina, but options like Ugin or the new Feroz are likewise tempting. Essentially, by playing solely 1-2 Planeswalkers in an Rx deck with Scrambles & Empower, you can hedge deckbuilding opportunity costs to access powerful soft tutoring. White meanwhile can just directly tutor Planeswalkers in a number of ways, including the brand-new Loyal Tutor, which means turbo Kasmina decks really want to be Bant, bare minimum. Black can do a bit of both of the above, Entomb-ing your Reality Scramble (they put Retrace on this card, can you believe that?) or directly tutoring relevant pieces, depending on your access to mana.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Hold on though, Empower Jace doesn’t say “that token”, it says merely to put Loyalty on a Jace token. Sure Kasmina’s a 2-card, but we can’t do that outside of a high Bracket 3 list—what nefarious lines might we use in a jankier Jace list? There are two Jaces which already make token copies of himself, but those are milquetoast, not worth funneling our Loyalty onto. Instead, we need to somehow copy him ourselves, ideally via our Commander; to that end, three candidates emerge, being Saheeli, Radiant Creator, Narset, Enlightened Exile, and in distant third, Nashi, Moon’s Legacy. Saheeli & Narset each have Red, meaning Scramble is on the table, but whether you prefer the mana efficiency of not needing to cast Jaces first with Narset or Saheeli’s UGx identity providing Kasmina is up to you. In either case, the two Jaces I’d look to turbo-tokenize are Jace, the Living Guildpact & Jace, Unraveler of Secrets. Each puts you insanely far ahead, and both have ults accessible via the magic number of 8 re:Jace’s Machinations. There are other Jaces you could consider, but for how invested you need to be to tokenize a Jace, it’s worth honing in on the best possible options. Empower Jace is a fantastic new mechanic to dive into, and between a powerful 2-card combo, Scramble synergies, and even enough jank to impress a Johnny like myself, there’s a lot to look forward to in Reality Fracture! I’m curious as to whether the Kasmina line actually makes it into fringe cEDH decks—Simic can always use smaller packages for wins, and without Black required it may end up as a worthwhile consideration for UGx, specifically Bant.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Conquest Meta Snapshot: Chios World Championship Predictions 2026
content:
If you’re a Conquest player, your eyes are either already on or will soon be drawn to the World Championships taking place soon in Chios. The qualifiers from across the world have been selected following many extremely strong performances in the last competitive season, with the Championships themselves taking place on the 28th and 29th of September.

As we noted in this article’s predecessor last year, even qualifying for an event like Chios takes a tremendous amount of hard work and skill, and every player present will be one of the best in the world. Winning an event like the world championships takes a tremendous amount of skill, at least a little bit of luck, and an understanding of and plan of attack for the prevailing metagame.

In this article we’ll be looking at that metagame and talk about how each faction is positioned to perform at Chios. Competitive balance in Conquest has improved markedly compared to some previous pre-Chios metagames, with even the strongest factions capable of being unseated and even the weakest factions in with at least a chance. As such, we’ve broken down the factions into three rough tiers: top-tier, middle-tier, and low-tier, rather than try to cleanly rank every faction in order. Factions will be roughly grouped within their tiers, but we need to emphasise that these overall groupings, and even the difference between strongest and weakest factions in the game, is currently pretty damn tight.

Top-Tier

Nords

While the gap between best and worst factions in the game is narrower than it’s been for some time, there are still at least a few factions that stand out as serious contenders, and first of those is Nords. While in terms of absolute mechanical power they don’t exceed either of the other top-tier armies, Nords sit at the top of the list by dint of the breadth of different list options they can bring that pack serious punch. Nords have one of the widest lists of powerful and transformative warlord options in the game, with serious contenders in the form of virtually all their options. The Volva remains as good as ever, and the Koungyr and Jarl both have interesting list options, but the Vargyr Lord and Shaman in particular have both emerged as serious top picks.

Of the two, the Vargyr Lord is a build-around warlord that produces an extremely powerful half-bloods list. Generally combining a high volume of werewargs and goltr, the Wild Beasts supremacy pushes the single most powerful ‘go turn’ in the game, with light werewargs connecting for extreme damage charge + clashes and medium goltr able to fill any gap or respond to any counterattack with march + charge + tramples. The sheer momentum this list sets off the supremacy turn, coupled with its extremely high scoring potential due to the early ground seized by so many lights and mediums, puts it in an extremely strong place into almost any matchup.

The Shaman, by comparison, is a consummate generalist. Virtually no list configuration fails to benefit from a Shaman, he’s an extremely efficient character just by himself, and taking him gives you full access to whatever might be the best fit for a list seeking to respond to other factions the Nord player considers the highest threat. Mountain Jotnar in particular are tremendously efficient medium monsters (when combined with the Shaman’s extremely cheap Jotun Shepard mastery, they’re just about the most cost-effective monster in the game), and Nord half-bloods and infantry all see reasonable place in a Shaman list. Even regiments like Huskarl, historically somewhat tricky to find a use for in the Nord roster, have potential as a high-defence meta pick against things like Sorcerer Kings ranged and spellcasting poke.

Sorcerer Kings

Credit Para Bellum Games

DISCLAIMER: This ranking and the subsequent assessment is based on two rulings previously confirmed by the rules team at Para Bellum but currently being re-litigated. These are that a Marid Sahar unit benefits from its own Aqueous Branding rule, but does not contribute to the maximum limit of three successful casts of the same spell under a Sorcerer Warlord’s Omnipotence ability. If either of these rulings change, move the Sorcerer Kings down, but only to the bottom of Top-Tier. Yes, free offensive spellcasting actions with a static wizard value on mainstay scoring regiments are that valuable.

Immediately after Nords, we have Sorcerer Kings. One of two factions that comprised the entirety of the competition-viable metagame in 2025, the hugely overperforming Fire Court-focused elements of the faction from 2025, and modestly overtuned Air Court monsters of early 2026, have both been brought down to earth, only to be replaced by the feature-complete, flexible and extremely powerful Court of Water. While the other courts (or a mix of them) remain viable in competition play under a Maharaja warlord, it’s the Court of Water that’s our pick for the most competitively dominant Sorcerer Kings army heading into the World Championship.

Core to the power of the Water Court are Marid Sahar, which still seem to be persistently slept on by some parts of the community. The underlying chassis for Marid is solid; decent stats, decent speed, decent offensive potential, and capable of fighting their way out of a scrap in a pinch. What makes Sahar one of the best units in the game is their Free Spellcasting Action, coupled with Aqueous Branding, and the relatively easily triggered automatic additional hits from Blood to Water. Free actions are always the most powerful ability to bolt to a unit in Conquest, and the tremendous flexibility and supplemental damage offered by a free Blood to Water means that Sahar are just outright one of the best units in the game. In practice, properly piloted Sahar perform like a more expensive but also more dangerous, durable, flexible, mainstay City States Chariot that can’t be neutralised by engaging it in close combat. They aren’t even particularly vulnerable to attrition, as a Sahar command stand with a single wound engaging the enemy still puts out a high number of spellcasting hits that cause resolve damage thanks to the static spellcasting value.

While three to five regiments of Sahar are powerful enough to form the backbone of a competition-viable army without too much assistance, the Marid Apsara and Shaytan have added a powerful heavy monster component to a pure water list as well, releasing in time to be legal for the World Championship. The Apsara is flexible and has some interesting force multiplication potential, but the Shaytan just straight kills things, bringing a huge volume of accurate, high cleave, terrifying attacks on a fast platform - effectively answering the one natural counter that high enemy armour poses to the high volume of hits Sahar are capable of meting out. They can be a bit vulnerable to enemy ranged attacks but are frustratingly difficult to bring down in melee, and overall serve as a perfect complement to their smaller brethren.

Put all of these together and you have a pure court list with access to the strongest rituals in faction and no capability gaps. The list constrains enemy movement with rituals (making approaching terrain a potentially lethal experience), exerts extreme medium-range offensive pressure with ranged attacks and spellcasting, can’t be countered by engaging it in melee, concentrates force excellently, has ample scoring units, is pleasingly quick once it’s on the board, and because it’s an easy pure court list to run, unlocks your choice of warlords to personal taste (using a Maharaja if you want to give Mahabarati an extra court bonus, but a Sorcerer or Raj otherwise). It even serviceably buffs both ranged output and defence, and heals very well with some setup (although most units will need ritual healing rather than spellcasting, as there’s little need for more than one or two Mortal units). Just an absolutely top shelf list, albeit without the faction breadth that categorises a faction like Nords.

Yoroni

Comprising the other fifty percent of the competition-viable metagame in 2025, Yoroni saw some developer attention over 2026, mostly to sidegrade their Geisha monsters to be still very good but no longer spammable brawler models with no downsides and no weaknesses. This has caused Yoroni lists to revert to a mix of old and new archetypes, which are still very strong off the back of the fundamental strength of modular regiments, good quality monsters and their highly flexible unique command stack mechanic. In short, it turns out it's quite hard to nerf a faction whose main power is that everyone is extremely dummy thicc.

While they fall at the bottom of the Top Tier factions due to lacking the breadth of list options of Nords or the sheer mechanical completeness of Water Court Sorcerer Kings, Yoroni lists still have a good mix of versatility and power. Modular regiments see play as both powerful brick units (with Mahotsu support, they are capable of putting up a shockingly durable brick that can lumbers into heavy engagement without many things seriously threatening it if it’s large enough), and as their usual fast, flexible, very dangerous, reasonably durable two-stand MSUs - in both cases forming an able backbone to any Yoroni list that can then be led and supplemented to taste by the Yoroni player.

The wildcard for Yoroni this year are the two Oni Kishin heavy cavalry units that have recently been added to the faction. Fast, durable, dangerous heavy regiments with a price tag to match, these are particularly noticeable for being heavy regiments with flank. This combination is extremely powerful and rare as it allows response to the first enemy medium regiment deployments with your own powerful counters without any risk of delaying your own deployment. The only downside these units have is that both the Oni Kishin Raiu and Kiba have a slight mechanical matchup issue into both Nords and Sorcerer Kings, since both can make heavy use of cavalry (Nord Goltr, Sorcerer Kings Marid Sahar, etc) which neither Oni Kishin units matches up into well mechanically (but can overwhelm with raw damage output).

Middle-Tier

Old Dominion

As we step from the Top Tier down into the Middle Tier, it’s worth reinforcing that all the factions here are still very capable, and where you draw that particular line really can vary from player to player. Straddling the boundary between tiers is the Old Dominion, who are sitting alongside Nords in terms of the potential breadth of warlord options and therefore lists they can play with their current roster. Virtually every warlord except the Theokrator is competitively viable (and the Theokrator is extremely viable as a standalone monster).

Personal favourite list archetypes include a Fallen Divinity list supplemented by extremely aggressive mortal light regiments (Cultists with Hierodeacons, and Hassasins - although Moroi and Kheres can perform here too), a generalist mixed-force creed and legion-based Archimandrite Warlord list with lots of dark power generation to fuel his power use, and frankly any of the martial characters to taste with a good mix of legion infantry and cavalry. Of these, we judge a list of legion medium regiments supplemented by a Theokrator as the most likely to see play at Chios, but if ever there was a year to see the Fallen Divinity present, this would be it.

Ultimately, despite their status as a casual meta boogeyman, we generally put Old Dominion at the top of the middle because much of their perceived power comes from new and inexperienced players not understanding how to play against them - but the overall force mix Old Dominion can presently access easily outweighs any very limited negative impacts from the recent introduction of the Brittle rule. Overall, Old Dominion are in that wonderful category of army where the most interesting thing about them is what dedicated faction players might unearth in the new rules and field to surprise their opponents at Chios, which marks them as a faction to watch.

Wadhrun

Wadrhun Matriarch Queens Conquest Credit: Magos Sockbert

Wadhrun are a faction sitting in a fascinating transitional space between old and new list ideas. Fundamentally, it needs to be acknowledged that the same Thunder Chieftain, Thunder Riders, speakers-centric list that’s been their competitive mainstay for multiple update cycles is still the competitive default, for all the same reasons it has been for all this time; it has outstanding lights, mediums and heavies that operate very effectively together, Winglord Predators remain outstanding for a wide variety of reasons, Hunting Packs with shock are the deadliest little goblin light unit in the game bar none, and the extreme threat range of Thunder Riders performing march + charge + tramples remains a coup de grace that’s difficult to play around but catastrophic if you don’t.

However, at this stage, the Thunder list archetype is a very known quantity. Any opponent is likely to have as much experience playing against it as a Wadhrun player is playing with it, meaning it’s an army that’s difficult for any but the most creative players to really pull off surprises with. That’s led to the search for alternate list archetypes for Wadhrun, and there are some promising candidates: the Scion of Conquest is capable of leading quite a wide variety of different list archetypes including more infantry-centric lists with things like Chieftains (who provide very capable buffs to their warbands and nearby units even when not the warlord), and a recent experimental but quite innovative Scion of Death list with multiple Matriarch Queens has emerged, which plays a very interesting game around just enough resilience mechanics (loose formation hunters winning ranged duels, chosen of death having their resolve shored up by the Queens themselves, etc) coupled with Matriarch healing for a list that’s more resilient than it looks at a first glance.

Overall, though, it’s still the Thunder Chieftain we’d most expect to see at Chios - but it will be extremely interesting to see if an alternate list emerges.

Weavers

Recent updates and releases have seen the Weavers recover wonderfully from the malaise of their initial release, with a roster that’s now really quite complete and with a variety of different options for competitive play. The two most likely competitive archetypes are actually built around units, not warlords, with Gallowglass Wardens and Warriors forming the backbone of one style of lists, and Wyrd Knights forming the other.

Gallowglass units are tough, capable, and the Wardens in particular play good host to any character that joins them thanks to their various ranged benefits applying in play rather than at list construction (meaning a Seanchas Sidhe for example effectively becomes a fourth Warden when shooting).

Wyrd Knights, on the other hand, are just straight up on cocaine. Evasion 2 and 4 wounds as a baseline defensive profile will always carry some risk especially from something like Marid Sahar, but the sheer speed, threat range and offensive output on a unit that are relatively easily accessible as a mainstay if needed, make them the basis of a very powerful archetype that pairs especially well with a Court of Spring Warlord, who also provides healing shore up any durability issues.

If there’s anything holding weavers back, it’s that even the better units on their roster are still pretty reasonably priced. Gallowglass aren’t cheap, their characters aren’t cheap, and while their light mainstays are cheap, you get what you pay for. There are also a few dead ends on the roster, with the Moth Rider cavalry having fallen off with small recent nerfs (the Ciannir Riders in particular having met the same grisly end as most other ranged units struck by the curse of exchanging Fluid Formation for Acute Senses), but the broad potential for an event-winning Weaver list certainly now exists, which represents an excellent change of fortune for the faction.

Dweghom

Dweghom Ancestor painted by Josh Gagel

Dweghom stormed into early 2026 in an extremely commanding position off the back of Magma Sorcery and Steelforged, both of which were subsequently nerfed, which has left the faction somewhat on the back foot looking to re-find its edge. Which, frankly, is probably… Magma Sorcery and Steelforged.

Steelforged, certainly, remain an absolutely outstanding unit even post-nerf. They’re reliant on Tempered Creed tokens but rarely struggle to fuel themselves in a properly configured list, and provided they can trigger one or both bonuses, are still the same ‘heavy regiment power on a medium regiment chassis’ that they’ve always been. That, in turn, means the Tempered Creed remains the optimal line for competition dweghom lists.

The choice of warlord, however, offers some versatility. Steelshaper and Tempered Sorcerer warlords are both very viable; the Steelshaper is generally excellent and the only meaningful source of healing in a faction that makes excellent use of it (even just chip healing to keep stands topped up is good in a faction with so much Defence 4). A Fire School Tempered Sorcerer is straightforward and strong. But for my money, I stand by post-nerf Magma Sorcery still being an extremely respectable competitive archetype on any list played table setups reasonably close to the tournament pack suggested terrain layouts. While it’s true that the magma death laser no longer gets to pick out any unit anywhere on the battlefield, the threat range of pyroclasts extending 6” in all directions from any Erupting terrain piece still presents an extreme zonal threat and the general ability to put damage on enemy units from a very long way away. This pressure in turn combines excellently with tempered list core elements (fireforged, steelforged, etc) to produce a powerful and consistent gameplan, albeit one that’s less powerful than it was in days of yore.

City States

Down toward the bottom of the middle tier but not quite edging into the low tier, we have the City States. Bad news: it’s still the Polemarch Warlord, folks, plus as many Chariots as you feel comfortable fitting. Good news: turns out those things are still really good; the Polemarch is one of the single best warlords in the entire game, and the general force composition of a City States list is very sound. It just hasn’t changed much in some time, putting it in the same ‘known quantity’ quandary as Wadhrun, but without any of Wadhrun’s promising alternate builds.

Where my read on City States differs from the broader wisdom is generally around the use of light troops. Quite common in the broader metagame are Thorakites units, usually with an embedded character and making excellent use of the Thyrean Auxiliary. And this is a very good unit, but I don’t think it’s positioned well into the top of the metagame. Against Nords and Sorcerer Kings, this unit setup is overwhelmingly likely to trade into a single enemy unit and, in doing so, trade down, unless you exert either the heroic effort or tactical nous to arrange for them to execute a second clash in a subsequent turn.

My personal preference as a result is for the use of Hoplites, which when led by a character (and frankly even without them) have the single best durability to points ratio of just about any unit in the entire game up to and including Steelforged. Paying 50pts for a Haspist Auxiliary nets you 7 wounds with Defence 4 Resolve 6 when a character is leading the unit, and at 35pts per further regular infantry stand, you can scale up defence faster than your opponents can scale up offence. This is an abuseable strength, but it doesn’t seem to have fully percolated into the broader community yet.

Around these pieces, the broader frills of the faction remain sound. Companion Cavalry are offensively cost-effective the same way Hoplites are defensively cost-effective; Inquisitors are well-rounded brutes, and while the various giants are slightly less cost-effective than their Nord Mountain Jotnar cousins, they’re at least within spitting distance with an added layer of utility and are therefore eminently solid.

For established City States players, the faction is feeling a bit long in the tooth by now ( the search for any non-Polemarch warlord is getting desperate), but the single list archetype with some variations remains competitively quite viable.

Low-Tier

Spires

Straddling the bottom of middle tier and the top of low tier, Spires are a faction who received a rework this year that took their previous faction identity built around complicated schemes, plans, buffs and debuffs and replaced it with a wide variety of ways to kill their own troops so the opposition doesn't have to (the typical expected value of which is left as an exercise to the reader).

However, notwithstanding that, there are a few strengths Spires can leverage to produce good results at an event. While virtually all units in the faction this side of Incarnate Sentinels are at least somewhat fragile and made more so by the need to carry wounds to activate their Strain abilities, there remain some units that are a serviceable mix of fast and dangerous. The Abomination in particular has become a cornerstone of Spires lists, and although it’s still very fragile by the standards of monsters, at 180pts it usually carries its weight. In addition, the recent change to the Directorate subfaction rules open it up as an alternative to Underspires for players who want higher risk and higher reward, with both being quite viable for competitive play (within the overall limits to the faction).

Overall, the biggest risk to Spires armies is generally Spires players themselves, as the faction’s fragility ruthlessly punishes mistakes - a Spires army generally struggles to survive errors in judgement, position or list construction (Merchant Princes are bad in competitive play; I will die on this hill). This creates a lot more scope for failure than success at an event as challenging as the World Championships, putting Spires close to the bottom of our meta snapshot, although by no means entirely out of the running.

Hundred Kingdoms

Hundred Kingdoms recently received a partial rework to accommodate new Orders regiments, which has left the faction in a slightly confused design space. The new regiments are serviceable enough; many Hundred Kingdoms are quite enthusiastic about the Martyrs of Saint Lazarus, for example, who are slightly inconsistent but overall still quite good human equivalent to Dweghom Flame Berserkers - but none will be legal in time for Chios list submission.

(In the case of the Order of the Sword: Good news for spectators.)

This leaves Hundred Kingdoms players looking to the existing model range, which is quite complete even without the new Orders regiment, but left somewhat discombobulated by a series of slightly confusing sidegrades and nerfs within the faction. An unexpected nerf to Battlefield Orders range has left the Imperial Officer edging ever closer to being the most useless character in the game once he’s actually deployed to the table, for example. Only a small number of rules and supremacies now make much use of the Feudal army rule to share keywords with their dynastic ally, and while a series of new warlord options have been introduced that represent a broadening of options, virtually all of which represent a small nerf in power compared to prior incarnations. Given the faction was reported to have the lowest win rate in the game prior to the update (although such statistics should always be taken with a large grain of salt), this begs the question as to what Hundred Kingdoms should be reaching for in competition play right now.

For our money, the most well-rounded competition list in the Hundred Kingdoms probably remains a Theist-Feudal alliance, with a Theist Priest Warlord (or dynastic ally). This alliance combination was already a well-rounded mix of durability, speed and hitting power, and it actually saw a small increase in power with the change to several Theist spells which can flow to the entire army during the Spirit Shines turn. In practice, setting up the full power of that fully armed and operational battlestation typically represents too many activations before the punching starts on a pivotal supremacy turn, but the high watermark has nevertheless risen and there are some additional interesting options with the new Theist spells outside the big go turn as well (being able to give Archangels Flurry, for example).

Even with the confusing downgrades and sidegrades to many of the Hundred Kingdoms’ subfaction combinations, it’s still absolutely conceivable that either a Theist Feudal list or some other dynastic alliance (an Order Warhorses list, for example) might appear at and even perform well at Chios. If we look all the way up to the top of the ladder, the difference between Hundred Kingdoms and Nords, Sorcerer Kings, Yoroni, Old Dominion etcetera isn’t that large. A list tooled in the right way, that’s ready for the opposition, in the hands of a practiced Hundred Kingdoms player still has a chip and a chair, which is a very positive thing to say about the game overall.
