title: Kings of War: Assembling Your Forces (of Nature)
content:
G’day tabletop battles readers! Welcome to the first in a new series of articles. In this series, I’ll be taking on Mantic’s Forces of Nature faction, getting a new army finished, from scratch, in time for Clash of Kings Australia in January next year.

I’ll be going through the new and old kits, building the models, hobbying them up, and learning how to play them.

So where do we start?

Who Are the Forces of Nature?

The Forces of Nature are a mix of factions united in the service to the Green Lady, Panithor's Goddess of Nature.

Based in the Forest of Galahir, The Green Lady commands the peoples of Men, Elves, Salamanders, Naiads, and, of course, Beastmen. These days, the alliances between these peoples are splintering, and only the Beastmen are staying truly united behind her.

On the Tabletop, the faction is split into two main parts. Firstly, the Herd. The part of the faction represents the various Beastmen peoples. These are the Centaurs, Minotaurs and the main people of the Herd, the Feraun. Think a more feline version of the classic half goat, half man. These units are generally fast, hard hitting, and low defence. They can dish out some pain, but can’t take it in return.

The second part of the Forces of Nature list are the Elementals. Led by various levels of Druids, the Elementals function in the opposite way to the Herd. Generally slow, and very tanky, they can grind down your opposition, but will struggle to reach objectives if you are not planning turns in advance.

Combined, the faction has a large number of playstyles available, depending on how you want to play and which list theme you’d like to lean into.

But given that, where do you start?

Mantic Games

Kings of War Champions

Luckily, I'm not the first person to ask this question.

If you're someone coming into ranks and flanks games for the first time, it can be intimidating to see full armies lined up. It's a lot of models that need to be built, painted and based, and what if you don't like the list you've built at the end of all that work?

Thankfully, Mantic have thought that through, and have an introductory game to both the world of Panithor and rank and flank games with Kings of War: Champions.

For those not in the know, Kings of War Champions is a small army version of the full size Kings of War. Rather than needing 12-18 units, that means potentially a hundred plus models, your force comes in one box. It is led by your Champion (hence the name) and usually you’ll get three other units, for around 20 models to paint. There’s variance here. For example, the Arokamorra Company Box (Ogres) only runs 8 models, so you can get them on the table very quickly, or take your time if you're just starting out.

If you noticed, I said it all comes in the one box, and that's right. There is no list building in Champions. You buy the box, and that's your company. This stops any indecision over how to build units, or painting a sixty model horde and realising it doesn’t work with your playstyle.

So, the Forces of Nature in Champions, what do we have?

Credit: Mantic Games

Ydrin Thorncreeper Company

Before I get into it, I want to thank Mantic for sending us this box to review.

Ydrin Thorncreeper. Photo Credit: Urr

Firstly we have Ydrin himself. He’s a MasterCraft Resin mini, the only non-plastic on in the box, and rightfully for a Champion, he looks great. The detail here is impressive, and goes together very nicely, with barely any gaps at all. There are a few mould lines to clean up, but none anywhere important or highly visible. The resin is a little more brittle than I was expecting, and I manage to snap his leg off cleaning up a tab, but that was fixed with superglue and now isn’t noticeable.

And then the rest of the company. One new sprue of hard plastic Centaurs, and two of Tribal Warriors. These are the full sprues, so both the ranged and melee versions of both units are available, though if you do want to build them for Champions, you will want to follow the instructions. The instruction booklet is not the most detailed, but still, seeing an instruction booklet at all is great, especially in an introductory product. There’s also a QR code to follow, that takes you to all Mantic’s build instructions online. This is a more detailed version of the booklet, if you need some extra guidance.

Loading...

Along with the sprues, we get the bases for the minis. These are Mantic's new modular plastic bases. In this box, we get the appropriate sized bases for two infantry troops, one cavalry troop, and Ydrin. These new bases come with connectors, allowing you to build up to bigger bases as required.

Finally, we have the faction cards. These are slightly larger than flashcard size, and have all the rules for your faction in a nice, easy to visualise way. We get one for each unit, and the faction orders. Once you know the main rules, everything you need for a new faction fits on said cards.

Now, if you are thinking of picking this up to get started in Champions or Kings of War, you don’t get any measuring devices or dice, this is just the faction pack. If you do want all the extras, Mantic do sell two player starter sets with those included, just have a look around, and make sure you know what you’re after.

Next Time

So, what is the rest of the plan? Join us next time and I’ll (hopefully!) have built the models, got some test paint schemes tried out, and some basing tests done as well.

The overall goal of this project is to bring a new, fully painted Force of Nature army to Clash of Kings Australia next year, and document the process. It is run in late January each year, giving me not a whole lot of time to get things done, but a challenge should be challenging!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: 7 things to expect in the Warhammer Big Autumn Preview stream
content:
This monday, Games Workshop replaced its normally scheduled model reveal with a preview of a preview, announcing the Big Autumn Warhammer Preview. The show will go live this Friday, September 18, and GW has hinted at reveals including the next Warhammer 40k codex and the (now thoroughly spoiled) Khazalite Holds for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. The teaser trailer for the show is packed with tantalizing logos which we've decoded to predict what's going to be revealed this Friday.

The preview itself goes live 11am PDT / 2pm EDT / 7pm BST on Twitch and YouTube. The WarCom article announcing the preview confirmed that we'll get reveals for the following games:

  • Warhammer 40k
  • Warhammer: Age of Sigmar
  • Warhammer Necromunda
  • Warhammer 40,000: Kill Team
  • Blood Bowl
  • Warhammer Quest: Darkwater
  • Warhammer: The Old World
  • Warhammer: The Horus Heresy

Holy Banana - Warhammer 40,000 - Adeptus Custodes

This high gothic inscription translates as 'in his name', but what's it written on? I initially took it to be a pair of pennants, the kind you'd find fluttering from a Sisters of Battle living saint. But on closer inspection I'm pretty sure it's a golden banana, and that's a sure sign of the Adeptus Custodes.

It's possible that more Horus Heresy minis are being revealed, but I think it's more likely to be the Custodes' 11th edition codex. The range has already been covertly refreshed via the Horus Heresy releases, and with the revision to Space Marine stats suddenly making them as tough as Custodes, there's a very good reason for GW to get the Custodes' codex out ASAP and ensure the Emperor's finest remain the most elite infantry faction in the game.

Rune of Valaya - Khazalite Holds for Warhammer Age of Sigmar

My heretic heart fluttered when I saw this intertwined V and inverted V, which collectively suggest both an XX and a pair of letter A's - an Alpha Legion Kill Team was looking likely! Then a smart Redditor pointed out that this is the Dwarven Master Rune of Valaya. So this is the faction symbol for the Khazalite Holds which were accidentally revealed by a website error on the weekend, and which GW confirmed when it announced the preview.

As an Old World Dwarf player, I'm delighted - as a traitor legion appreciator, I'm disappointed. Still, every model is an Alpha Legion model if you've got the will and the green stuff.

Flaming Skull - Necromunda - House Cawdor

I have sad news for Legion of the Damned fans - the undead Space Marine chapter's logo is just a skull, with no flaming aura. The flaming skull belongs to House Cawdor of Necromunda. Given how incredibly crisp the new sculpts for houses Escher and Goliath have been, this should be impressive.

Corpse Starch - Warhammer 40,000: Kill Team - Specialist Astra Militarum

Corpse Starch is the final destination of the average Imperial citizen on any hive world, and the tabletop game Necromunda features both the Mercator Pallidus corpse merchants and the insane Corpse Grinder cults. The only reason I think this is actually a Kill Team reveal is that it would be too obvious.

Well, not just that - I think GW is going to reveal new minis for the six main Houses before it moves onto the niche gangs. The Astra Militarum eats a fair share of Corpse Starch, and this sure looks like a ration tin, particularly as the stencil font is very close to one used on the Astra Militarum vehicle transfer sheet.

The most obvious Guard kit in need of an update is the Catachan Jungle Fighters, but - as we've seen with Spectre Squad - GW isn't above inventing new teams when it wants to!

Nehekhara 4 Life - Tomb Kings Star Players - Blood Bowl

Nehekhara is the domain of the Tomb Kings in both Warhammer: The Old World and the comedy parallel universe where Blood Bowl takes place. The fact that this graffiti is so silly suggests that this is a teaser for the gridiron. The Tomb Kings launched with Blood Bowl Third Season edition, and so far there are no star players themed around them.

II - Astartes 2

Since Space Marine 2 came out in 2024, the only "2" that Warhammer fans care about is Astartes 2, the long-awaited sequel to Syama Pedersen's seminal CGI animation. Presumably we'll get an updated teaser trailer and details of when it launches. This year, we hope!

Squig Herd - The Old World or Warhammer Quest Darkwater

This is the prediction I'm least certain about. This is unquestionably a herd of squigs, the kind that Night Goblins and Gloomspite Gits alike prod into battle. The fact there's a sword stuck in one says this isn't anything to do with Blood Bowl. But what game are they part of?

The Old World range is, technically, missing any official Squig Herd or Squig Rider models. But the Age of Sigmar models work really well for the job: the Squig Herd minis fit onto 25mm bases and rank up pretty well, while the skirmishing Squig Hoppers don't actually need to rank up very often.

GW does release new designs for The Old World that fill a very similar niche to Age of Sigmar models, as with the recent Chaos Knights. I just find it very, very hard to picture what that could be for the Night Goblins and particularly the squig hoppers. Their AoS aesthetic is almost identical to their Old World identity - angry meatballs.

The alternative is that the next Warhammer Quest: Darkwater expansion will feature gobbos. How would they fit into the battle for the Jade Abbey? It's obviously 'dank', and therefore prime real estate for the Gloomspite Gits. And the game is set up to be easily expandable with new encounter cards and monster stat cards. But it feels like a peculiar turn after the dramatic battle against Nurgle in the base game.

What do you think is coming? What about the games where there's no obvious teaser? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: [40k] Warhammer Legends Is Fine, Actually
content:
You’ve probably seen posts like these. A lot of posts like these. You might even have made posts like these. Attached to these you may have also heard the term Legends used like a four letter word, and not one of the fun four letter words, but like, the really bad ones. A lot of this vitriol comes from a fundamental misunderstanding of what Legends is and why units get Legends rules. My goal here today is to clear up those misunderstandings and maybe, just maybe, tone down the salt levels a little bit.

The Video Version

If you'd rather listen to my dulcet tones and watch some cool models spin around, check out the video version of this piece instead over on our YouTube channel:

What Is Warhammer Legends?

Let’s just define what Legends is and isn’t before we dig in too much. While Legends sort of existed for old Warhammer Fantasy armies after the transition to Age of Sigmar, Legends as we know it was introduced back in 2019 for 40k, in a post on Warhammer Community:

 “As codexes are revised and editions (and eons) pass, classic models become unavailable, no longer finding their way into current publications. Rather than consign these battleworn relics to oblivion at the back of your shelves, however, we are happy to present them as Warhammer Legends.”

“...these profiles will not be curated as part of the annual points review, and as such aren’t really intended for use in competitive play (unless, you know, you want to organise an event where Legends are welcome).”

So that seems pretty cut and dry, right? They’re rules for old models that GW doesn’t make anymore, they won’t get regular points reviews, and they aren’t meant for competitive play unless you want your event to include them. That post is archived and seven years old at this point, but the goal still remains the same: Providing points and rules for units that GW isn’t supporting anymore. That is not the same as removing a unit from the game or adding it to a ban list, just keeping it out of tournament play specifically.

Now there’s a second, newer thing introduced in a recent Warcom post called Legendary Proxies. That’s basically just taking old models and running them as a modern equivalent, with some pretty similar stipulations: 

“As with Legends rules, Legendary Proxies can be used at home, in stores, clubs, and campaigns, but if attending a competitive Warhammer event, these units should only be used with the permission of the event organiser.”

I’ve got a little exercise for you. Now I’m going to need you to look into your mind palace and picture what I’m about to tell you. Picture a squad of Space Marines. Each of them is holding a massive bolt pistol in one hand and a chainsword in the other. On their backs are huge jump packs so they can leap into combat. Were you picturing these?

Black Templars Assault Marines. Credit: SRM

Or were you picturing these?

Rainbow Warriors Jump Pack Intercessors by Craig "MasterSlowPoke" Sniffen

Either way, you’re right. Some people get mad about these but really, how angry can you really be that your rules for a Marine with a boltgun are now the rules for a Marine with a boltgun? The names have changed and maybe some equipment is different, but that’s the only material difference here, and you’re not being asked to do anything else. I’ll even let you keep calling them Tactical Marines if you’d like. I still say Imperial Guard and Eldar; it’s fine, nobody cares. 

Why Do Units Go to Legends?

The first question most people ask when a unit goes to Legends is “why”. Sometimes these are newer models, like the Hammerfall Bunker, or models that started as Legends units to begin with, like most tie-in models from Black Library books. There’s a few reasons, mostly boiling down to kinda boring business reasons and game design considerations.

The simple, mundane reason units go to Legends is because they just stop making the kit. Molds for plastic kits wear out and are expensive to replace, and unless it’s a kit that will obviously sell enough to justify making another mold, like the ubiquitous Rhino, then it might go to Legends. Sometimes it’ll get a new kit instead, like that new, slightly different Intercessor kit coming out, but this is one of the main reasons they stop supporting a unit with new rules - they just aren’t selling it anymore. 

Another consideration is game design and balance. There are hundreds of Datasheets, with more being added all the time. Considering how often the game gets balance updates and new Codexes, that’s a lot of datasheets to maintain. If you have a boring database job you probably understand how tedious maintaining that many assets is, and how that scope can make for a snowballing amount of work every time they want to update something. You might say they shouldn’t update the game as often as they do, and you’re allowed to think that, I just remember people who had to wait 12 years for new a Dark Eldar codex.

Boomdakka Snazzwagon. Credit: Rockfish

The last is redundancy. Sometimes units get straight up replaced with something that does more or less the same job, or a unit gets an updated model with different equipment options. In the new Ork Codex, a bunch of the vehicles from Speed Freeks got condensed into a generic warbuggies sheet, but can you really tell me the material difference between a Kustom Boosta Blasta and a Boomdakka Snazzwagon? Would you even know the difference if they were on the table next to each other? They both go fast and shoot stuff, it’s fine. Games Workshop is always going to put out new models - it’s what they’ve been doing for over 40 years - and that’s going to mean some stuff gets pushed to the side to make way for the new stuff. 

Why Does Legends Make People Big Mad?

From the way you hear people talking about it, you’d think Legends was a program where Games Workshop thugs personally came to your house and smashed your old models with hammers. While Legends isn’t as drastic as deleting something from the game forever, it does mean those units aren’t usable in tournaments anymore. I’ve got a bombshell for you though, so make sure you’re sitting down: Not being allowed for tournament play probably doesn’t affect you. Before you scroll to the bottom of the article and fill that comment section with descriptions of specific objects and where I should shove them, let me go over some data. Now there isn’t perfect reporting on what the whole community is like, but we have run reader surveys here, and respondents are going to be by their nature pretty engaged members of the wargaming community. After all, these are going to be the kind of people who keep up with our daily coverage of the wide world of wargaming.

In those surveys, we’ve found that more than half of our readers play less than one game a month, and less than a third of our readers had been to a tournament that year. Even then, most of those who do go to events only go to maybe one or two a year. This isn't meant as any sort of insult to people who don't go to tournaments or play more often, but more of a reality check. If Legends just prohibits units from being used in tournaments, this doesn’t affect those people at all. Statistics say: this probably shouldn’t matter to you either.

Now if this does affect you because you’re a heavy tournament player: Hey, me too. I’m one of our resident competitive sickos, and most of my games are either at tournaments or prepping for tournaments. I’m the exact kind of person this affects the most, but also, as a tournament player, I’m used to changing up my list to stay on top of the meta already. If this describes you too, my heart goes out to you - when the main format you play doesn’t allow you to use your models, that sucks. There’s no sugarcoating that; it’s just another meta you need to keep up with.

Oldhammer Meets 8th Edition. Credit: SRM and Dylan Gould

Some people also are going to be upset that they can’t buy those old units anymore, and I don’t have much good news for them either. The secondary market has only gotten more expensive, and as someone who used to collect a lot of old out of production stuff, I know that game. Some people have armies with a specific look that relies on a certain kit that is on its way out, and yeah, that’s gonna be tough. Models go out of production every so often, no matter the game or even the manufacturer.

The reason I imagine most people get upset at a unit being sent to Legends is because they feel it devalues the work they put into their own units. You put all this time and effort into a Tactical Squad and their Razorback, of course you still want rules to play with them. It’s also something that’s unusual in the miniatures gaming space. While trading card games like Magic the Gathering or Pokémon regularly cycle out old sets, you’re not spending 20 hours converting and painting your trading cards, and it's just part of the game that most people understand. Miniatures games have largely been exempt from that sort of churn. Warmachine did something similar, but outside of that, people are pretty used to using their old models all they like. After all, at no point did Napoleon introduce a Primaris brigade and send his Voltiguers to Legends, and I can still use the BattleTech minis my dad painted in the 80s, even if handling them is going to give me lead poisoning. 

Watching Out for Legends

The minute Primaris Marines were introduced back in 2017, I knew that the days of short king Marines were numbered. You don’t start releasing parallel, more advanced versions of existing units without a long term plan to phase out the old ones. Even though Vindicators were pretty hot in tournament play for a while, I wasn’t painting any because I had the inkling that since they were a firstborn Marine kit from 2008, they were gonna get sent to Legends before too long, and since I play in a lot of tournaments, I didn’t want to feel like my efforts would be wasted. I’m not sharing these anecdotes to toot my own horn or because I want an award for being the smartest boy - I’ve been barking up that tree for years and my therapist still hasn’t given me one - but because I want to educate folks who maybe don’t recognize these patterns to think on them a little bit. If Legends is something you really, genuinely want to avoid, having some understanding of what gets models sent there might prevent some heartache down the road. 

Kitbashed Black Templars Marshal. Credit: SRM

The first one you’ll want to watch out for is models that require any sort of kitbashing to come together. Games Workshop isn’t in the business of making rules for models they don’t produce, unlike the old days where you might get a codex page with a bunch of wargear you had to convert up or kitbash. That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t kitbash your own models, it’s a ton of fun, but if something doesn’t have a model or you’re banking on some gear that doesn’t come in the stock kit, it’s something you should probably avoid.

The next is pretty obvious but requires some research, and that’s old models. I’m genuinely shocked that the Land Raider didn’t get sent to Legends since that kit is 26 years old. Most of the kits that get relegated to Legends are ones that are older, usually because after a certain point GW stops making them, like the more obscure old tanks from Forgeworld. Based on how recent Necromunda and Specialist Games releases have been, I’d also probably avoid anything resin, since it seems like they’re really trying to pivot completely to plastic. Again, great looking models, but unless you have an easy proxy or genuinely don’t care about Legends, I’d probably avoid picking up a new $500 resin child.

Ciaphas Cain & Jurgen. Credit: Games Workshop/Warhammer Community

Another common factor for Legends units is when they’re explicitly based on Black Library books. Ciaphas Cain and Ferren Areios started as Legends models, while others like Ufthak Blackhawk had rules usable in tournaments before ending up in Legends too. This has been a bit more recent of a change, but I think the best way to think of these is as collector’s models you get just because they’re neat, and maybe you can use them as something else. Pick up Hell’s Last because you want a cool command squad or you like the Minka Lesk books, not because you’re expecting them to have explicit rules for tournament play.

What to Do with Your Legends Units

Credit: Kevin Stillman

Uriel Ventris got sent to Legends? Oh no! Now how am I going to use the man with the most chopped haircut on Macragge? If only there was some way you could take a Space Marine Captain with a power sword and a boltgun! The point here is that ol’ squaretoes here has an obvious analogue, and so do a lot of other Legends units, usually because they’re older or parallel versions of something else already there. Other times they might be characters with wargear that isn’t supported by the new kits, in which case, there’s no rules requiring you to model your exact wargear, so your old metal Autarch can just be armed with whatever you want. It ain’t perfect but it’ll let you keep using your Finecast blorbo for years to come.

Legendary Proxies are also pretty easy. Honestly, Suppressors becoming proxies for Inceptors is the best thing to happen to them in years. The game designers already did the work for you, so keep on using the units you like if they’ve got a ready proxy. And if not, materially, does it really matter that you have to use the Cadian Guardsmen rules for your Mordians or Valhallans? It’s a guy in flak armor with a lasgun, if Cadia can stand, so can Vostroya. 

Rainbow Warriors Chaplain on Bike by Craig "MasterSlowPoke" Sniffen

Another thing you might have noticed is that a lot of old Legends units tend to come back. The biker Chaplain peeled out with that initial Legends announcement 2019 and came back in 2020 with a bigger bike. Rough Riders didn't take too much longer. Huge chunks of the Stormcast and Skaven ranges for Age of Sigmar went to Legends in April 2024, only to come right back in June when their ranges got updated. If one of your units goes to Legends and you can’t or don’t want to play with Legends units, you can just hold onto them and wait until later when they probably return. Sometimes that might mean rebasing them to match whatever the newer version of their model is. As far as hobby projects go that’s not a particularly fun one, but it’s not exactly a hard one either. If an old vehicle gets a new version, you can also make a base that matches the new footprint too.

Ultramarines vs. Emperor's Children at the Tacoma Open 2026. Credit: SRM

See that 2nd edition Rhino over there on the right side of the board? It’s on a base the same size as a modern Rhino, and I played against it at the Tacoma Open, a Games Workshop-operated Grand Tournament. Nobody had any problems, and everyone was cool with it. If you ever have questions about that sort of thing, you can follow the advice in the original posts that Games Workshop made and just contact the event organizers. Whether that’s a GW event or an independent one, they’re hobbyists just like you and are generally gonna be pretty permissive.

The last thing to do with Legends units is: Use them! Just use them! They’re legal outside of tournaments, and unless you’re playing in a tournament, bust out your weird old models and go to town. If you’re not sure, ask your opponent beforehand, and they’ll probably say yes. Most Legends units aren’t even that good on account of not being regularly balanced, so it’s not like you’re trying to powergame here, and if you’re not in a tournament you probably don’t care about running the most optimal units anyway. Maybe that’s the invitation your opponent needs to break out their own old Forgeworld model that hasn’t seen the table in the last decade. If you’re so inclined or you’re a narrative player, you can even homebrew your own rules or adapt an old datasheet to the new edition, just again, run that by your opponent. Narrative events also usually allow Legends. Games Workshop’s own Grand Narratives and the Narratives at the Warhammer Open events all allow Legends, no questions asked. In case you’re worried that we don’t put our money where our mouths are either, when we run Narratives at the Tabletop Battles Open, we allow Legends units there too. Outside of tournaments, the only person stopping you from using these models is you. Take your little lead pals out of their cases, break out those obscure tie-in models, and go play some Warhammer. 

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? title: Lore Explainer: The Rings of Power in Tolkien's Work
content:
Three Rings for the Elven-kings under the sky,

Seven for the Dwarf-lords in their halls of stone,

Nine for Mortal Men doomed to die,

One for the Dark Lord on his dark throne

In the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie.

One Ring to rule them all, One Ring to find them,

One Ring to bring them all and in the darkness bind them

In the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie.

- Epigraph to The Lord of the Rings
NB: This explainer post deals with solid canon from The Lord of the Rings, The Hobbit, and The Silmarillion, and other supplementary material written by JRR Tolkien. The TV series is separate semi-canon; I haven’t seen it, and I don’t feel it’s relevant to this particular discussion.

The One Ring - Credit Peter J Yost. CC BY-SA 4.0

As the name of the books suggests, the Rings of Power are at the very core of the Lord of the Rings’ narrative, but what are they? Where did they come from? What do they do? To answer these questions, we need to cast our minds back to the dying days of the First Age of Middle-Earth (we’ll discuss exactly what happened in each age in a different article; keep an eye out for it). Morgoth, aka Melkor, aka Middle-Earth’s Lucifer, finally did enough evil deeds to the men and elves of Arda that the rest of the Valar (best understood as kind of archangels - again, we’ll discuss the cosmology of Arda in another article) had enough and came to give him a damn good shoeing. They succeeded in beating up their errant cousin and pushing him through the Door of Night into “the void,” but in the process they made a real mess of the land of Middle-Earth, sinking the westernmost part (called Beleriand) beneath the sea. Oops. The Valar didn’t quite succeed in destroying all the evil, though. One of Melkor’s lieutenants by the name of Sauron (a Maiar) managed to escape and go to ground for a while, along with a whole lot of Orcs, some dragons, a bunch of Balrogs, etc. That’s right, the Big Bad in The Lord of the Rings got his start as a lackey of Middle-Earth Satan. 

In the interim, numerous realms sprang up across Middle-Earth: Elven, Dwarven, and Human. A polity of elves known as Gwaith-i-Mirdain inhabited an area west of the Misty Mountains known as Eregion, where they were ruled by the extremely handy artisan-lord Celebrimbor. Geographically, Eregion borders the Dwarven kingdom of Khazad-Dum/Moria, and the elves of Eregion cooperated closely with Durin’s folk to their mutual benefit - Celebrimbor crafted the magical doors of Moria (the same ones that the Fellowship find their way through by solving the “Speak Friend, and Enter” riddle). By the time of The Lord of the Rings, all that remains of Eregion is the ruins seen by the Fellowship as they travel south from Rivendell. 

After spending a good five hundred years laying low, Sauron came to the conclusion that the Valar had stopped looking for him, and so the heat was probably off. No longer fearing being beaten up and shoved into the void with his master, Sauron embarked on his grand scheme to dominate the world. Being a very powerful Maiar, Sauron had little difficulty corrupting the already-sort-of-corrupt men of the east and south (awkward implication alert) and bent them to his will. With these men under his control, he began the construction of his own realm in the east - the land of Mordor.

Ready to enact the next stage of his plan, Sauron put on a pretty face and went to introduce himself to the Elves, disguised, acting naturally, and going by the name Annatar (Gift Lord). The Elven ruler of Lindon, a mighty king named Gil-Galad, was not at all convinced by the Annatar disguise and told Sauron to hit the bricks and get lost. Undeterred, Sauron/Annatar visited the elves of Eregion and offered to teach them some special ancient elven crafting secrets for their next project. This offer was apparently enough for Celebrimbor to invite Sauron- I mean Annatar into Eregion. Since Annatar/Sauron was a master manipulator, he proposed the creation of magic rings that would help each of the species, bringing peace and prosperity to the various species of Middle-Earth. In secret, he mixed a bit of hocus-pocus into the creation process, meaning that the rings would be able to act on the desires of the wearer and twist them to Sauron’s benefit. Sauron’s ultimate trump card would be the creation of a master ring, which he alone would control. Wearing this master ring would allow him to activate the poison pill buried in each ring’s creation and dominate the mind of the wearer, turning them into his puppets.

The elves of Eregion made an unknown number of so–called Lesser Rings, both as trials and as practise, but when we’re talking about The Rings, we’re talking about the major rings.

As detailed in the poem above, if you add ‘em all up, twenty rings of power were produced through the collaboration of Celebrimbor and Sauron/Annatar, each intended to be presented to the rulers of kingdoms and sorted by species; so let’s have a look at them that way, shall we?

Galadriel. Credit: Rich Nutter

The Elves

Celebrimbor made the three elven rings by himself, with knowledge gained from Annatar, but without the Dark Lord ever having actually touched the rings or been personally involved in their creation. Because Sauron never actually handled the rings, his power over them is lesser compared to the rest of the rings; conversely, having learned about them, he was gripped with a very strong desire to possess the three. Since the rings act on the desires of their wearer, and what the elves desired most was to stop their decline, each of the Elven rings has the power to alter the flow of time and create a kind of stasis bubble that arrests or slows change, allowing the elves to live in peaceful elven enclaves, protected from the alteration of the outside world.

The uncorrupted nature of the three, combined with the insight of the elves in the first place, allowed them to react quickly after the completion of the One Ring; they heard Sauron’s voice in their heads and yanked the rings off tout-suite. What do you do with magic rings that perform a really desirable function when worn, but are talking to you inside your head? The elves chose to hide the rings in safe places until Sauron was apparently defeated at the Siege of Barad-Dur. With the owner of the One Ring turned into a kind of ghost, the Elven lords felt safe enough to put the rings back on and keep their enclaves lovely once more.

The three elven rings were:

Nenya - The Ring of Adamant or the Ring of Water - worn by the Elven Lady Galadriel and used to maintain the elven enclave of Lothlorien. When Galadriel wears the ring, it’s normally invisible; only Frodo (and presumably Gandalf, as another ringbearer) are able to see it. The power of Nenya centred around protection, preservation, and concealment from evil. 

Narya - The Ruby Ring, or the Ring of Fire - originally worn by Cirdan the Shipwright, the Lord of the Grey Havens, later given to Gandalf (who isn’t an elf, but that doesn’t seem to matter).

Vilya - The Sapphire Ring, or the Ring of Air - originally worn by the King of Lindon, Gil-Galad, and after his death at the hands of Sauron, worn by Elrond and used to maintain Rivendell.

Why would Cirdan hand over such a powerful artefact? When Gandalf was dispatched along with the rest of the squad of Wizards on their mission to defeat Sauron, he arrived at the Grey Havens. Cirdan, having the power of foresight, saw something in Gandalf and was moved to offer him the powerful ring, saying:

"Take this ring, master, [...] for your labours will be heavy; but it will support you in the weariness that you have taken upon yourself. For this is the Ring of Fire, and with it you may rekindle hearts in a world that grows chill." - J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Third Age"

From this we can assume that the power of Narya grants the wearer an increased ability to inspire hope and courage in others, which makes Gandalf an ideal bearer after all. Presumably ol’ Cirdan saw that too.

Medbury Dwarves - Completed Group - Credit Thundercloud

Dwarves

The Dwarf Lords received seven rings in total, six from Annatar, and one from Celebrimbor himself. Of these, we only really know details of the latter, known as the Ring of Thror. When Sauron sprung his trap, he found that the Dwarves were annoyingly resistant to his mental domination - possibly because, unlike men and elves, dwarves were not created by Eru Ilúvatar, but by the Valar Aulë. While he was unable to dominate the dwarves and therefore impose his will on them, the rings still worked for them.

The rings worn by the Dwarven Kings boosted their innate technical skill, ambition, and desire for wealth, making them avaricious and extremely wealthy, allegedly giving them the power to multiply whatever ores, jewels, and metals they mined. While that may sound like a positive outcome for the Children of Durin, you really have to be careful what you wish for, don’t you? See, amassing enormous hoards of treasures, gold, and jewels has a habit of calling down and attracting the only creatures that are as obsessed with gold and jewels as Dwarves: Dragons. It’s almost as if there’s an invisible treasure-o-meter that goes up the more you gather in one place, until ding ding, dragon time. One by one, the holds of the dwarven clans were attacked, ransacked, and eaten by the giant fire-breathing lizards, their holds serving as big dens for the kleptomaniac beasties. As a result, most of the Dwarven rings were destroyed when the dragons chowed down on their bearers.

The Ring of Thror was a little different, though, being given by Celebrimbor as a gift to King Durin III of Khazad-Dum and passed down to his heirs before gracing the hand of Thror, the King of Erebor, the Lonely Mountain. We’re all familiar with the arrival and subsequent conquest of the Lonely Mountain by the dragon Smaug - rather than being eaten like the other Dwarven Kings, Thror actually managed to escape and lived in exile, passing the ring to his son Thrain, the father of Thorin Oakenshield. Thrain and his kin moved to the Blue Mountains. However, Thrain grew increasingly obsessed with the lost wealth of Erebor (probably a result of the ring he was wearing), launching an expedition to reclaim the mountain; as the band of dwarves camped under the eaves of Mirkwood, Thrain disappeared. Gandalf later found that Thrain had been captured by agents of Sauron and taken to his hidden citadel at Dol Guldur, there he was tortured, the ring and finger cut off, and he was left to die - Gandalf found a much diminished and mentally incapable Thrain in the dungeons of Dol Guldur, from whom he received the map and key that acted as the catalysts for Thorin’s quest in The Hobbit.

Earnur, Last King of Gondor (otherwise known as Aragorn, King Elessar from Wish) - credit Warhammer Community

Men

The race of men received the greatest number of rings from Sauron, nine in total. We don’t really have any details about these particular rings; Tolkien kept it vague and didn’t elaborate all that much on the rings or their wearers - we know that three of their number were Numenoreans, while another (the only one with an actual given name, Khamûl) was an Easterling. The rings were given to kings, sorcerers, and mighty warriors, and through their power, the men all achieved wealth and glory. Lacking the insight of the elves or the alien mental fortitude of the Dwarves, these men were easy prey for the mental domination of Sauron, and quickly fell under his spell, losing themselves piece by piece, before becoming inhuman, invisible wraiths and Sauron’s greatest lieutenants - the Nazgûl, or Ringwraiths. 

Credit: Games Workshop

The One Ring

Sauron’s masterwork, the One Ring is a fairly unassuming ring - described as being a perfect circle of unadorned gold, appealing in its perfection of form, but not ornamented or set with any stones. Unlike the other rings of power, Celebrimbor and the elves had no input in its creation; Sauron fashioned the ring alone in the fires of the volcano Orodruin (aka Mount Doom) in the corrupted land of Mordor, and as Galadriel says in the prologue to Fellowship of the Ring: “Into this ring he poured his cruelty, his malice, and his will to dominate all life.” 

When Sauron slips the finished One Ring on his finger, it acts as a sort of antenna for his psychic domination, with the remaining Rings of Power acting as conduits, connecting Sauron to the other bearers. As mentioned before, the perspicacity and insight of the Elves enabled them to intuit what was happening and pull the rings off in time to avoid being mentally overwhelmed. The Dwarves, with their unusual minds and general resistance to psychic mumbo-jumbo, were largely unaffected by the domination power of The One Ring, and ultimately only the bearers of the Race of Men were fully captured and corrupted by the powers of the ring. 

When worn by mortals, the One Ring confers invisibility by moving the wearer into a wraithlike parallel world that ordinary creatures can’t see; conversely, wearing the ring renders the bearer extremely visible to other “unseen” creatures, like the Ringwraiths and Sauron himself. Owning the ring extends the bearer’s lifespan dramatically (Gollum was almost 600 years old when he died; Bilbo is quite spritely and appears relatively young at his 111th birthday party - an age at which Hobbits could be described as “pretty elderly”, and ultimately lived to 131 - and even then he didn’t “die”, but sailed west with Gandalf and Frodo) while causing a severe physical and mental dependence in the manner of an addict. Gollum, who spent 500+ years with the ring, is so dependent upon it that he can scarcely live without it; all his thoughts are utterly consumed with it. Bilbo owned the ring for a comparatively shorter time, and is able to give it up (with some difficulty) to his nephew Frodo. Even so, when Frodo brings the ring to Rivendell, Bilbo has a hard time keeping his desire in check (yes, that part in the film where Bilbo’s face goes all scary and he goes “Graaar!” is in the book). 

The One Ring manipulates its bearers, exerting a kind of psychic pressure on them, attempting to bend their will towards helping it return to Sauron. Ultimately, the ring “wants” to return to Sauron and be reunited with him. Despite being an inanimate object, in my opinion, the One Ring appears to have some kind of limited sentience (debates have raged on this topic since at least the 1960s), making decisions and taking actions (abandoning Isildur at a critical moment, abandoning Gollum at a critical moment) that display some kind of strategic thinking, but as I said, it’s an inanimate object, the only physical thing it can “do” seems to making itself fall off someone’s finger at an opportune moment. 

While its physical actions are extremely limited, its abilities to manipulate and poison the mind of the bearer are very much in line with Sauron’s own abilities as a master manipulator. If a normal human had worn the ring, they would probably have succumbed to the temptations in short order and marched immediately against Mordor, inadvertently delivering the ring to Sauron one way or another. The corrupting power of the ring is so singular that, had a powerful elf like Galadriel or Elrond worn the ring, they would still have been captured by its manipulations and gripped by the desire to become a dark lord themselves, as Galadriel herself says:

“And now at last it comes. You will give me the Ring freely! In place of the Dark Lord you will set up a Queen. And I shall not be dark, but beautiful and terrible as the Morning and the Night! Fair as the Sea and the Sun and the Snow upon the Mountain! Dreadful as the Storm and the Lightning! Stronger than the foundations of the earth. All shall love me and despair!”

 - The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, Chapter 7 “The Mirror of Galadriel”

So if the corrupting power of the ring is so impossibly strong, why were Bilbo, Frodo (and Sam) able to bear and wear the ring without being corrupted? The answer is a little convoluted. Despite being a subspecies of Men, Hobbits aren’t possessed by any strong desire towards power, wealth, or greatness - their general contentedness (petty concerns and squabbles aside) means that the Ring doesn’t have as much to “latch onto”, giving the Hobbits a kind of natural resistance to its manipulative effect. That’s not to say that Hobbits aren’t tempted by the ring - When Frodo is out for the count at Cirith Ungol, timely intervention by Sam stops the ring from falling into the hands of the Orcs and he wears it on a chain around his neck, the ring acts on him and shows him visions as a mighty hero who destroys Sauron and becomes the world’s greatest gardener.

Even so, against Hobbit resilience, the corrupting effect of the ring is only delayed, rather than averted - Gollum was a Hobbit once, before centuries of exposure to the One Ring irreparably damaged his mind and body. Despite this damage, Gollum never turned into a wraith, but was able to endure the presence of the ring for five centuries.

Mount Doom and Barad-dûr, as illustrated by J.R.R. Tolkien

In the later parts of The Lord of the Rings, the Ring - perhaps being “aware” that it was coming closer and closer to Mordor and Sauron - begins to inflict a heavier physical and mental toll on Frodo, rendering him closer to Gollum and further from the untainted Sam (who bore the ring for a short time, but never actually wore it). The ring’s corrupting effect increases the closer the bearer comes to Mount Doom, becoming overwhelming. Indeed, at the critical moment, Frodo is unable to destroy the ring. In his letters, Tolkien explains that at the place of its creation the power of the ring would be so immense that no one would have been able to destroy the ring:

“I do not think that Frodo's was a moral failure. At the last moment the pressure of the Ring would reach its maximum - impossible, I should have said, for any one to resist, certainly after long possession, months of increasing torment, and when starved and exhausted. Frodo had done what he could and spent himself completely (as an instrument of Providence) and had produced a situation in which the object of his quest could be achieved. His humility (with which he began) and his sufferings were justly rewarded by the highest honour; and his exercise of patience and mercy towards Gollum gained him Mercy: his failure was redressed.”

- JRR Tolkien, Letter 246.

Ultimately, the ring is destroyed not by Frodo’s action, but by Gollum’s inability to let the ring go as the result of centuries of corruption and dependence. 

Once the One Ring is destroyed, the other Rings of Power lose their magic and become useless as well, and all of their effects begin to dwindle at once. Bilbo’s physical age rapidly begins to catch up to his real age, leaving him old and frail upon Frodo’s return to Rivendell. The elven rings cease to function, and their preservation of the elven refuges begins to falter, causing rapid depopulation as their inhabitants make their way to the Grey Havens and the ships to take them to the Undying Lands. A century after the destruction of the ring, Arwen goes to Lothlorien to die and finds it in ruins, silent and empty. The ringbearers (Galadriel, Bilbo, Frodo, Gandalf, and Elrond), no longer needed, depart the Grey Havens for the Undying Lands on the White Ship. Sam follows them later, before Cirdan (once a ringbearer), his task as the guy who operates the metaphysical ferry port at an end, builds the Last Ship and follows them.

Note: The nature of the ring itself changed quite dramatically between the first publication of The Hobbit and the conception of The Lord of the Rings. In early editions of The Hobbit, the One Ring is what it appears to be: a magic ring that conveys invisibility, serving as a plot contrivance to help Bilbo survive later dangers. Bilbo acquires the ring as a prize for besting Gollum in the game of riddles; Gollum gives up the ring willingly, shows the way out of the Goblin cave, and Bilbo continues on his merry way. During the writing of The Lord of the Rings, a decade or so later, Tolkien realised that, in the context of The Lord of the Rings, through its corruption, Gollum would never be able to give up the ring willingly, and so revised the original text. In the new (much more familiar text), Bilbo finds the ring and uses it to escape Gollum, who is trying to find and kill him. The Lord of the Rings reveals that the ring sensed the reemergence of Sauron in Dol Guldur and “abandoned” Gollum in order to hitch a lift with a new “victim”, one conveniently headed in the same general direction as Dol Guldur. title: Magical Athlete is a stupidly smart board game, powered by pure nonsense
content:
Our Verdict

Believe the hype. Magical Athlete is a bizarre, visually entrancing, left-field masterpiece, transforming an old, tedious dice mechanic into a carnival of chaos that'll delight anyone and everyone at your table.

Pros
  • Simple yet delicious gameplay
  • Hilarious characters make everyone smile
  • Stunningly effective nostalgic art
Cons
  • No real strategy
  • M.O.U.T.H. may cause nightmares

Here's a riddle for you: what do you get if you take Chutes and Ladders; set it in a dreamlike, primary-colored 1970s kids' cartoon that never actually existed; make each piece an adorably painted little wooden weirdo; give them all chaotic abilities that make every race an unpredictable nonsense; and then throw it all into a gorgeous, oversaturated box for just $30? You get one of the best board games ever made, that's what.

Let's be real: you've already heard about Magical Athlete. It's been a while since one board game created this much buzz on the BoardGameGeek forums, in board gaming Reddit, at cons, or at your local game store or gaming café. If you're into board games enough to be reading this, someone has already told you about the bizarre racing game that's somehow made 'roll and move' - the least cool board game mechanic ever - into the latest tabletop sensation.

I'm late to the party, but I'm not alone in that, because this thing has been tough to get hold of, selling out all over, multiple times, since it hit shelves ahead of 2025's holiday season. After playing two back to back games at my local café, I immediately bull-rushed the front desk to buy it, and the salesperson commended my fortunate timing; my copy was one of five they had left, from a shipment of 200. Their second shipment of 200. Even if they were exaggerating a bit, these are not ordinary numbers.

1/3

What with this, and designer Jon Perry's unhinged, mascot-racing betting game Hot Streak, both making absolute bank, I hope CMYK - the publisher of both games - has upped its staff party budget this year. I can't imagine the non-stop rush of orders its poor logistics folks have had to field!

In some ways, the hype is not surprising. Magical Athlete is a reimplementation of Takashi Ishida's pretty obscure 2003 game of the same name - and the designer of this updated version is some guy named Richard Garfield, who apparently invented a card game called "Magic: The Gathering".

That kind of origin story is bound to attract attention (and, if you're reading this, Richard, we'd love to interview you about it). Magical Athlete's outstanding, instantly enchanting art style, created by artist Angela Kirkwood, also makes it physically impossible to walk past this game on a store shelf without picking it up - on which more later.

But still, a roll and move race game? In 2026? Are we just pretending the last 40 years of progress in board game design never happened? Is this just a vibes-only, nostalgic passion project that looks pretty and quirky, but fundamentally won't see much play for anyone above the age of eight?

Short answer: no. Long answer: no, and I'm pretty sure it'll be remembered as one of the biggest design trendsetters of the decade. Let's talk about how Magical Athlete takes board games back to absolute basics, then elevates those basics to an absurdist artform.

How Magical Athlete plays

Magical Athlete's board is a linear racetrack of spaces. You'll draft racers from the 36-strong roster, place your pieces at the beginning, and race to the end by rolling one six-sided dice each turn, and moving your piece that many spaces forwards. First and second place finishers win points; the player with the most points at the end of four races wins.

Oh, and halfway through you flip the board from the default, unobstructed 'Mild Mile' track to the 'Wild Wilds' side, which is spiced up with Chutes and Ladders-style special spaces: jump ahead X spaces; jump back X spaces; trip over and miss a go; get an extra point. That's it, that's the game.

Only joking! There's more, of course - but it's essential to understand that, structurally, that really is it. It's just a race. The magic of the game is in its athletes: the huge cast of goofy characters who'll be running this race, each with their own unique in-game effect.

Without exception, each ability is extremely simple on its own, though anyone familiar with playing Magic: The Gathering will quickly sense its influence in the straightforward, yet measured wordings: some are "can" abilities; others always happen on a given trigger, like landing on another racer's space; yet others are always-on 'passive' abilities.

Other than suiting their owners down to the ground, having a silly joke name noted at the bottom of each racer's card, and consistently making Bonkers Things Happen, the main thing all 36 abilities have in common is that they have nothing in common.

Veterans of strategy games (and especially MTG) will instinctively be looking for balance and, sure, you'll find some within each ability; the most powerful ones are all curbed by randomness or luck-pushing.

The Genius above, for example, can theoretically take infinite turns! But only if you correctly predict which number you're going to roll, each and every time. The Flip Flop (who is a flip-flop) can use its 'Flop Flip' ability to swap places with any racer - which is mega powerful if you're behind and useless if ahead.

Between racers, however, the 'power level', if you want to try and call it that, is essentially pandemonium. Sisyphus, the poor sod, gets thrown back all the way to the beginning every time he rolls a six - but he'll grant you a few extra victory point chits at the end (unless he's very unlucky).

Meanwhile M.O.U.T.H. (pictured above), the most terrifying racer in the game, straight up eats any other racer he lands on, disqualifying them from the race instantly. Legs (see below, he's got really big legs) can always move five instead of rolling - usually very powerful. The adorable, two inch thick Huge Baby (see below, he's a huge baby) bumps back anyone trying to land on his space. All racers are not created equal.

In fact, perhaps predictably, a lot of the thrilling jeopardy here comes from abilities that do nasty things when racers land on other racers' spaces, combining abilities that manipulate other racers' move distances. Like Gunk, the snot green monstrosity above, whose 'Goop 'em' passive ability makes everybody but them move one space fewer. Or racers like the Magician and Dicemonger, who bring re-rolls into the mix.

The genius behind this madness is that the particular brand of chaos in each race is dependent on the specific combinations of racers in play. You can affect that somewhat through your drafting decisions at the beginning - the only real strategic decision you'll make in the whole game. But each player's chosen racer for each round is revealed simultaneously before its starting gun, so any sense of controlling the game as it goes along is loose at best, and your ability to 'counterplay' is very limited.

As a result, trying to do any meaningful strategy or planning across the course of a game is, by design, a folly. And yet - as the absolute legends at Shut Up And Sit Down rightly say in their own glowing review above - Magical Athlete gives you just enough of a hint of a ghost of a feeling of control, that you never disengage; it never feels like you're watching rather than playing.

In the addled, blurry mental state this game will induce in you, you somehow always feel this close to getting a Pro Play away, even as its satisfying diversity of racer matchups and simple, but hilarious rule interactions gives you more and more evidence that you're only riding this wacky minecart, not driving it.

This makes a universally accessible, ridiculously simple, mostly random, dice rolling race feel like a Proper Board Game™️, and keeps even hardcore gamers' rapt attention glued to the board at all times. That stupendous mind trick is half of what makes Magical Athlete an exceptional game for literally anyone, regardless of board gaming experience.

The other half? Come on, use your eyes!

How Magical Athlete looks

This game is right up there with The Old King's Crown among the best looking board games I've ever set my peepers on. Magical Athlete's box contains only a few things - a board, a rules booklet, and two paper bags containing the printed wooden racers, wooden dice, and cardboard points tokens - and the moment I opened the box and looked at them I started grinning uncontrollably.

Every single item is maximally jazzed out with Scottish illustrator Angela Kirkwood's vivid, joyful characters and an in-your-face, kids' TV color palette. Comparisons between Magical Athlete and the simplistic drawing styles, buoyant happiness, and bright block colors of pre-millennium children's cartoons are obvious - but there's a definite bite of unnerving absurdism too.

Kirkwood's gaggle of gorgeous, weird little guys immediately put me in mind of The Beatles' 1968 animated movie musical Yellow Submarine - one of my personal childhood favorites, watched dozens of times on a battered VHS recorded off the TV.

Quite a few of the characters seem to share DNA with the psychedelic, art-nouveau-inspired weirdos drawn for that movie by Heinz Edelmann and George Dunning over half a century ago. A lot (though not all) of the racers have hysterically exaggerated body shapes and enormous teeth that are, unarguably, giving 'Blue Meanie'. If you know, you know.

Inevitably, for me, that juices up this game's top-to-bottom retro vibe. But it also underlines the 'Alice in Wonderland' effect of its setting and characters - in that they feel simultaneously cutesy, and low-key a little bit terrifying. You might say I'm overthinking it, but scroll up, have another look at M.O.U.T.H., and then come back and tell me so.

This all works so, so well. It's a perfect aesthetic match for a game whose appeal is offering something extremely simple - harking back to an innocent, complexity free childhood - but hiding something compelling underneath that's gripping for grown ups too.

More importantly, as with all the best games, the theme and visuals are inseparable from the gameplay. The game is the characters, and vice versa. Magical Athlete is a complete, coherent package where what you see is:

  • What you get.
  • Crazy town banana pants.
  • Very, very good indeed.

Why you should buy Magical Athlete

We give out 10/10 scores rarely on Wargamer. In our review scale, a 10 represents a best-in-class game: something that's near faultless, is the best game of its kind upon release, and leads the industry in at least one important way.

That rubric occasionally runs into trouble in board game land, where it can be difficult to define 'kinds' or 'genres'. But, fundamentally, if a game is magnificent in its own right, if it does what it does better than any other game we've played, and if what it does is exciting, worthwhile, and wildly playable - it's going to be a contender for a perfect score.

If it manages that level of quality, and also opens new avenues for the medium, or makes a meaningful statement about what board games can be - and especially if it's extremely accessible to new gamers - these things can also help us to justify a 10.

Magical Athlete is among the easiest 10/10s I've ever approved. It invents a mission for itself - taking the most basic possible board game format and making it sing - and then achieves it elegantly by augmenting dice rolls with endlessly entertaining, semi-random player interactions. Angela Kirkwood's terrific artworks then turn it from a fascinating game design experiment into a bona fide phenomenon.

I wouldn't claim it's entirely in a class of its own. At the simplest level, it's a low-effort party game that plays with an old-school, kiddy concept, adapting it for adults with clever, measured rules and stylish visuals. Lots of new games have done that - notably The Fuzzies, Wavelength, and Monikers, all also published by CMYK.

But the thing is, Magical Athlete is simultaneously stupider, smarter, and better than those games. There's something profound about taking roll and move, and making it able to intrigue and captivate not only people who generally play the likes of Luthier or Brass: Birmingham, but also those people's kids. The last board game I gave a perfect score to was The Old King's Crown, a fairly complicated, multi-layered strategy game stacked with mechanics and interlocking options. I love that stuff. Magical Athlete is in many ways the exact opposite, and I wasn't expecting to like it, really. Yet here I am, grinning away, awarding it 10/10.

That's why I say this is likely to be a trendsetter: if Ishida and Garfield's game can set the scene on fire with just a colorful D6 and a paper bag full of wooden oddballs, it's a fair bet other designers are going to try and remix dead-simple kids' stuff into nostalgia-fueled modern classics, too. I say, let them try - we could all do with a bit more nonsensical joy in our lives. But boy, oh boy, Magical Athlete is going to take some beating. 

For more over-enthusiastic ramblings (or to chastise me for them) come join the free Wargamer Discord community, where we're chatting tabletop games seven days a week.
