title: Blood Bowl Season 3: Underworld Denizens Team Guide
content:
If you like your Blood Bowl ultra-violent, full of fouls, touchdowns, Star Players, and general insanity, then we have the team for you!  Underworld were one of the game’s boogeymen in the early days of Second Season, as their access to Swarming Snotlings, great Star Players, and strong individual positionals made them the perfect cheap chassis for tournament cheese.  After a succession of nerfs and changes, they’ve slipped under the radar somewhat, but they still have a tremendously varied roster and a unique flavour (or should that be smell?) that makes them one of the most interesting, flexible, and effective teams in the game.  In this team guide we’re going to run through all of their many options and sort the sewer rats from the biological waste.

Pros

  • Extremely flexible and varied roster that can be built for any play environment.
  • The Gutter Runner and Skaven Blitzer are two of the best positionals in the game.
  • Powerful fouling and Star Player support.

Cons

  • Many squishy players.
  • No redundancy in positionals.
  • Lots of different rules and pieces that need to be coached in harmony.

The Roster

Goblin Linemen

The hunched backbone of the Underworld team, the Goblin is a familiar and not very impressive sight.  Underworld Goblins have one major advantage over their conventional peers: Access to Mutation skills on Primary.  That means very fun possibilities like Two-Heads letting Goblins go anywhere on an unmodified 2+.

In practice, Dodge and Stunty will often prove to be extremely useful tools in general play, with the former being a very powerful defensive tool against unskilled opposition players, and the latter allowing for unique re-positioning (and occasionally offensive) opportunities.  And if nothing else, Goblins also make great foulers, so Devious skills like Dirty Player and Lone Fouler are great choices for them.

Snotling Linemen

Snotlings painted by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms (Joey K)

Underworld Snotlings lost one of their most important tools in Third Season, with Swarming being taken away from the team.  So why continue to take the weakest and most easily injured player in the game?  Well Snotlings do have some saving graces; Dodge and Sidestep mean they can actually be extremely annoying to pin down, and the Stunty and Titchy combo means they can dodge anywhere on a 2+.  They are also astonishingly cheap, at 15k a pop, which means they are your best tool for fouling, risk-wise.

Snots also gained access to the new Devious skills category in Third Season, which means a plethora of fouling and annoyance skills are within easy reach.  While they also get access to Mutation skills on Primary, there’s not much appealing for them.  Not skilling Snotlings is probably the best plan, as it more than doubles their cost and doesn’t give you much in return, but Dirty Player and Lone Fouler are definitely options, while Diving Tackle has strong synergy with Dodge and Sidestep, and can lock down weak and unlucky opponents.

Skaven Clanrat

Skaven Lineman by @7s_and_2s on Instagram

The third of the Linemen on the Underworld team is the Skaven.  For the most part these are exactly the same as those on the regular Skaven roster, which means they are good all-rounders, with very high movement, but a little lightly armoured.  Despite that, they will end up doing a lot of marking and line of scrimmage work, simply because you have no one else who can reliably do it.

Clanrats can be built in many different ways, and Mutations are also an option.  Wrestle and Block are the most solid options (with Wrestle cheaper and probably preferred in Third Season).

Skaven Thrower

Skaven Thrower by @7s_and_2s on Instagram

The Skaven Thrower is one of two main options as ball carrier on the roster.  With Sure Hands, PA2+, and Pass, he easily pick the ball up and move it on to other players as required.  With that role in mind, the Thrower generally needs to be kept out of trouble and might want to sit out defensive drives.

Block is a good development skill for Throwers that keeps them alive and can let them contribute more on both sides of the ball.  Dodge is a Secondary but another great survival and mobility option.  Leader is a very cheap reroll, but thanks to the nature of Underworld team building, you arguably won’t need more of those outside of tournament settings.  Extra Arms is another good option that synergises with Sure Hands for pickups in difficult circumstances.  +MA and +AG are good stat ups.

Skaven Blitzer

This boy got quite the glowup in Third Season, getting an extra point of MA and the Strip Ball skill, making what was already one of your best two players into a bonafide out-of-the-box star.  Underworld lean heavily on the Blitzer as their only truly reliably blitz option, so using it effectively will be one of the main skills to master as an Underworld coach.  Ideally, it should be kept free of contact so that it can use its huge movement range to blitz, or support an advancing Gutter Runner each turn.

Tackle or Mighty Blow are probably the strongest first skills for Blitzers, helping them be even better at their primary role.  Guard is a good general support option, while Mutation access allows Claws, which is also a good first skill, but even better in combination with Mighty Blow.  Break Tackle is another strong option that enhances their mobility even further.  All of the stat ups apart from +PA are also excellent options for Blitzers.

Skaven Gutter Runner

Skaven Gutter Runner by @7s_and_2s on Instagram

Amongst a team of assorted and sometimes dubious merits, the Gutter Runner is your touchdown-getter par excellence.  MA9 will often leave even experienced coaches saying “he can move how far?!” as it races out of trouble and toward the endzone.  With Dodge and AG2+ it is perfectly equipped for its role and is unquestionably the most important and precious player in your entire team.

Accordingly, keeping it safe is your number one challenge.  Unlike the Gutters on the Skaven roster, trying to use your lone Gutter as a ball-hawk is a dangerous proposition.  You may even chose not to field it on defensive drives, especially if you plan to lean into bashing and fouling.  Using the gutter to score on your own drive, and then using it  to try a two-turn or one-turn touchdown after your opponent’s drive is a perfectly valid strategic approach.

So, how do you improve the best scoring threat in the whole game?  Well perhaps I could offer you Two Heads?  Extra Arms?  Yes, Gutters also get access to Mutations, and as if they weren’t spoiled for skill choice before they are now.  Sidestep, Block, Dodge, Hit and Run, and Sprint are all great options.

Trolls

Blood Bowl Trolls (sculpted by BruteFun) painted by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms (Joey K)

The first of our Big Guy options is the Troll, as seen on numerous other greenskin teams.  And the Troll has all the benefits and drawbacks we have come to love(?).  It is strong, tough, and cheap; but they are slow, and Really Stupid is one of the worst negatraits, meaning they require constant babysitting to accomplish anything.  Unlike other teams’ Trolls. Underworld retained Loner on theirs in Third Season, making them just as risky and unreliable as ever.  

Did someone say Tentacles?!  Yes, just like everyone else on the team, Underworld Trolls can take Mutations as Primary skills.  Claw is another that can really enhance their killing power and make opponents hesitant to base them.  Otherwise, as always, Trolls benefit hugely from Block, though it is a Secondary, as it helps them stay on their feet and prevents turnovers.  Guard is a good old reliable option, while Stand Firm can also add to the roadblock role.  If you want to lean into throwing team-mates, Bullseye is a fun new option in Third Season.

Rat Ogre

If the Troll is the roadblock option, then the Rat Ogre is the bulldozer.  Blitz, blitz, blitz is the tactic of choice for Roger, and in a team that lacks muscle and blocking power, the Rat Ogre certainly delivers it.  The downside as always is higher fragility, and the possibility to injure your own players with Animal Savagery.

Rat Ogres benefit the most from either Juggernaut or Block to provide a safety net for their blitzes.  Juggernaut also has some additional utility.  After that, Claws and Break Tackle can up their killing power and mobility respectively.  Guard is also an option, but Frenzy and Animal Savagery can make positioning Guard problematic.

Star Players

Hakflem Skuttlespike, Blood Bowl Star Player painted by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms (Joey K)

The Underworld Challenge Star Player pool got a little shakeup in Third Season, losing a former UW favourite in Varag Ghoulchewer.  However, it still has a superb selection of some of the most impactful stars at various price points.  That includes the likes of Bomber Dribblesnot, Fungus the Loon, Glart Smashrip, Ripper Bolgrot, and the two super-gutters, Hakflem Skuttlespike and Skitter Stab-Stab.  This selection allows you to tailor your team to any opponent or fill any hole or need you have.  Gutter Runner MNG’ed?  Then take Hakflem or Skitter.  Facing AV10+?  Glart is your guy.  Cut-price mayhem?  The Goblins have you covered.

This is one of the strongest areas for Underworld, and be it in tournament or league play, you are likely to find yourself with star support, so make sure to familiarise yourself with their various strengths and their particular special rules.

Tactics and Playstyle

Blood Bowl Goblin Troll by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

Underworld can be played and built in many different ways, but primarily they play somewhere between a heavyweight Stunty team and lightweight Hybrid team.  This means you want to exploit your movement and mobility, and use your blitzes and fouls as surgical tools, rather than heavily basing-up your opponent.  With multiple Dodge and Stunty pieces, and extremely fast Skaven players, Underworld are able to escape bashy opponents and reposition the whole team easily.  You can outmaneuver most opponents while trying to pick off their more influential and important players.

Fouling is one of their strongest tactics, so in a typical turn, a Blitz on a valuable opponent with either a Rat Ogre or Skaven Blitzer, followed by a Snotling or Goblin foul, is a good approach.  Remember also that Underworld have the Bribery and Corruption team rule, which means that once per game you can reroll a 1 on Argue The Call, and Bribes become a very good inducement option at 50k each.

On defense you will have to make a call on whether nor not to field your strong ball-players, The Gutter and Thrower, which will give you a much bigger chance of making a defensive score, or let them sit out and just lean into punishing your opponent.  There's no right or wrong answer here, but if your opponent has nasty Gutter-hunting pieces (anything with block/mighty blow/tackle) or likes fouling, then just consider the risk to your own offensive drive (and season!).

With a Gutter Runner (and optional Frenzy Big Guy) and/or Throw-Team options available, one-turn touchdowns are a huge potential play for Underworld.  Moreover, if you have both threats on the table, your opponent will not as easily be able to set up to defend against a particular one.  These can be complicated to set up (and certainly dice-dependent to accomplish) so you will again need to do your research and practice to make sure you are ready for the opportunity.

Starting Team Builds

Blood Bowl Star Player, Glart Smashrip painted by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms (Joey K)

Underworld have a multitude of options for team building in every environment.  You can build them at very low TV and lean into the inducement game, or aim higher and have a deeper roster.  For league play we’ll do the latter, and then look at some cheesier tournament options.

League Play

  • 1 x Rat Ogre
  • 1 x Skaven Thrower
  • 1 x Skaven Blitzer
  • 1 x Gutter Runner
  • 3 x Skaven Linemen
  • 4 x Goblin Linemen
  • 5 x Snotling Linemen
  • 3 x Team Rerolls

This comes to a round 1m GC, and gives you 16 bodies to feed into the meat grinder.  You could also drop 1 Snotling to buy two additional Dedicated Fans which will generate more cash for inevitable replacements during the season.

League Development

For the above build only the Apothecary needs to be added to the mix (and reserved probably exclusively for the Gutter Runner).  Any other spare cash can be used for replacements.  Keeping the team lean will give you more inducement cash down the road, allowing you to add powerful stars and bribes as desired.

Tournament Play

  • 1 x Rat Ogre
  • 1 x Skaven Thrower
  • 1 x Skaven Blitzer
  • 1 x Gutter Runner
  • 3 x Skaven Linemen
  • 4 x Goblin Linemen
  • 3 x Snotling Linemen
  • 2 x Team Rerolls

This is a cheap 900TV shell that lets you play the inducement game.  At 14 players it will let you take up to 2 stars (assuming your tournament pack allows it).  You can use a skill to get Leader to bump up the rerolls.  You can make it even cheaper by swapping the Troll in for the Rat Ogre, but if you do this I would look to ensure you take a good blitzing star like Glart.  You can tweak this roster very precisely for your tourney pack so that you can get hold of particular inducements.  Some strong options at various price points include:

  • 130k Bomber or Fungus + 1 bribe
  • 175k Glart
  • 180k Bomber or Fungus + 2 Bribes
  • 250k Ripper
  • 255k Glart + Bomber or Fungus

Tournament Skills

Priorities for skilling are the Gutter, Blitzer, Rat Ogre, and Thrower.  If your pack gives Secondary skills then Block on the Rat Ogre (or Troll) is a good use of it.  Otherwise take Juggernaut (or Guard on a Troll).  If skill stacking is allowed, The Gutter and Blitzer can make great use of it.  Combos like Block/Sidestep on the Gutter or Mighty Blow/Tackle and Mighty Blow/Claw on the Blitzer can be extremely powerful.  Wrestle clanrats are an excellent tool both defensively and offensively, and a Goblin with Dirty Player or Lone Fouler, and another with Two Heads, will be very useful.

Tier

GW have kept Underworld in Tier 1 in Third Season, and this largely reflects their potential for shenanigans when given more cash and star options in lower tiers in tourney play.  Nevertheless, they remain a very strong team whose flexibility means that coaches can carefully curate the team to meet their playstyle and the threats of their meta.

title: Necromunday: N26 Gang Tactics Compendium
content:
Greetings scummers! Previously Gang Tactics were a bit of a mess, and many campaigns (including the ones run by us at our Necromunda Weekender events) simply refused to use them. N26 has brought them back and it’s worth taking a look and seeing what’s changed. 

Gang Tactics are one of the more controversial parts of Necromunda. Depending on how you look at things they’re either a fun way to incorporate randomness into the game, a potential balancing mechanism, or a horrifying exemplar of bloat and poor game design that were best left abandoned in a ditch full of flaming promethium. In the previous edition Gang Tactics could do everything from force an opponent’s top player to miss a game, randomly double the size of a gang from a series of added fighters, or do absolutely nothing. Modifying how Gang Tactics worked became one of the most common Arbitrator decisions, and generally players either curated a small table of tactics that they would draw from or the Arbitrator would limit what was available. For example, in the 2026 Necromunda Weekender held in Maryland we let everyone get access to two uses of Adrenaline Surge. Other campaigns just don’t use them at all.

How Gang Tactics Work in N26

Gang Tactics are used as a balancing mechanism within N26. Gangs are limited to a number of randomly generated tactics based on the presence of leaders and champions, and as part of the Pre-Battle Sequence each player selects on Gang Tactic that they have access to. For every full 200 credits difference between Gang Ratings the player with the lowest Gang Rating may select one additional Gang Tactic that they have access to. Gang Tactics can only be used once per battle.

How Gang Tactics Are Acquired

Gang Tactics are generated by either adding Leaders or Champions to a roster or by performing the Develop Tactics action. Adding a Leader generates two Gang Tactics, while each Champion generates an additional Gang Tactic. For a standard gang that includes a Leader and two Champions, that means players will have access to four Gang Tactics. During the Post-Cycle Sequence Leaders and Champions have the option to perform the Develop Tactics action, which allows a new Gang Tactic to be randomly generated. It should be noted that this action competes with all of the other major actions such as Medical Escort or Visit Trading Post, meaning that there is a significant opportunity cost behind generating another Gang Tactic.

When generating a Gang Tactic, players select from the available tables and then randomly generate which tactic they get. In the event that they select a tactic they already have then must re-roll. Everyone has access to the Core Gang Tactics in the main rulebook, which provides a total of 18 skills with an equal chance of being obtained. Those with Gang books, such as House of Chains, have an additional six skills to choose from on a separate table. 

Core Gang Tactics

The Core Gang Tactics range from amazing all the way down to so situational you might as well not bother. Of the 18 Gang Tactics, ten appear to be relevant to a given gang depending on if they're melee or ranged focused. Six are generally applicable to any gang, while there are a solid four that seem like they're going to the kind that people will immediately regret rolling. Notably none of the Gang Tactics are absolutely useless; that tier is reserved for one of the House Gang Tactics.

We find that the most valuable Gang Tactics are those that provide a reliable source of additional activations, such as Adrenaline Surge and Desperate Effort. Rapid Healing, which allows even a Seriously Injured Fighter to regain a Wound, is also extremely valuable since changing the Status and Injured Condition seems to immediately allow the Fighter to act normally. On the other side Grenade Bouquet could be fun but it requires grenades (and proximity to the opponent), while Burst of Courage has a relatively minor benefit since Bottle Checks are very different in this edition.

There are also two Gang Tactics that we think Games Workshop might need to address in an upcoming FAQ. Chain Attack explicitly allows a Fighter to perform a Charge action after previously performing the Fight action, but it does not say if you would be allowed to perform a second Fight action after charging. Rapid Fire lets you perform the Shoot action as a Free action, but if combined with the Fast Shot skill it could potentially mean a Fighter could shoot twice for free and still perform two actions. That seems a bit excessive.

Loading...

Soggy's Escher Gang

Escher Gang Tactics

Escher lucked out with a healthy number of useful Gang Tactics. Chem Queen is particularly fantastic, as it gives a free Chem-alchemy Elixer stimm to any Fighter before they activate. There's no restriction on how the player uses this ability, so they could give Blood Rush to anyone or use one of the melee focused stimulants at a crucial time. All of the other skills are at least somewhat useful, although Three-point Landing would naturally only work on a table with vertical elements. Still, it's pretty cool to think that a Fighter could jump down six stories and do a superhero landing.

Loading...

Converted Goliath Forge-born with Hand Flamer credit: Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

Goliath Gang Tactics

Where the Escher got a bunch of really nice tactics, the Goliath... well there's a reason we have an "Utter Trash" category. Crunch Time gives all "hand weapons" a +1S and the Concussive (5+) trait. The problem is that "hand weapons" literally mean a weapon from your hand, and depending on how you read the core rules a Fighter with a weapon with the Melee or Light trait might not even have access to it. Most weapons are generally better than the upgraded punches. On the plus side, Force of Habit lets you use skills if a Fighter is Injured which could potentially help a medic heal themselves. Ironhide can also help reduce the threat from a high power weapon, turning the Lethality of a melta into a lasgun.

Loading...

Arbitrator Suggestions

One of the biggest issues with running a Necromunda campaign is limiting the number of moments where a player feels bad because of things completely out of their control. Necromunda is not a balanced game, and while randomness makes sense for things like taking shots or seeing if a Fighter falls to their death, it can be crippling when one player randomly rolls three amazing Gang Tactics and another player gets absolute crap. This is particularly egregious because Gang Tactics are intended to be a balancing mechanism.

One possible solution would be to just let players choose what Gang Tactics they like or let everyone get access to Adrenaline Surge and then have them roll for the other three. It may also be a good idea to not require Fighters to perform post-cycle actions to roll for new Gang Tactics; the opportunity cost versus visiting the Trading Post is huge and the team that's going to need those extra Gang Tactics is likely going to be the one least likely to get them. Instead, Arbitrators could consider picking the extra Gang Tactics for the downtrodden gang, or mix it up and include fun options like Grenade Bouquette with a free Demolition Charge.

Wrapping Up

Something to consider is that N26 is very new and we're still figuring out exactly how different the game is from previous editions. We've seen a lot of reports that the game is significantly less lethal than previous editions, which may alter how Gang Tactics pan out over time. We also fully expect that Games Workshop will adjust things through FAQs and errata, and as that happens, we'll keep this article updated. In the same way that we did with N23, we will also add to this article as new gang books are provided.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Warhammer 40k's new Space Marine rules make Guilliman as hard to kill as a daemon primarch
content:
Games Workshop has previewed the first new Space Marine dataslates ahead of their 11th edition codex release, and if you play another Warhammer 40k army, you might want to brace yourself. GW had already foreshadowed a power boost for the Space Marines that would make the army play more like the elite force that's depicted in the novels - it didn't warn us that Roboute Guilliman was going to be as hard to kill as a daemon primarch.

 

Guilliman has clearly spent a lot of time polishing the Armour of Fate, because he's now Toughness 10, has 16 wounds, and gains Feel No Pain 5+. That's still two less Toughness than Mortarion, daemon primarch of the Death Guard. But he's also one quarter the size of Mortarion, and as such he gains the Lone Operative ability while he's within 3″ of a friendly Adeptus Astartes unit, meaning units more than 12″ away can't shoot at him until they wipe out his screen.

Guilliman will be just as hard to kill as his brother, but in different match ups: melee armies will chop up Guilliman more easily than Mortarion when they reach him, but he'll have a far easier time hiding from long range shooting. Of course, that's only for the time being: I have to assume the Lord of Death's reworked 11th edition datasheet will be even more imposing.

One surprising aspect of Guilliman's datasheet is that it is, very slightly, simpler than the 10th edition one. Guilliman's 'Author of the Codex' ability used to give him a choice of three unique special abilities each round: now it just lets him select one Combat Doctrine and apply it to a friendly unit for the round. He no longer has the ability to (potentially) resurrect upon death - he just gets six extra wounds. And his ability to reduce the Command Point cost for a unit using a Stratagem is now just a bonus CP each round, and it's a rule that also appears on Captains.

He does have a couple of new abilities, but they're simple enough - he gains the benefit of all three Combat Doctrines at all times, and he projects an aura that lets friendly Astartes models reroll rolls of one to hit and to wound. I'm glad to see a reroll aura stapled to Guilliman, specifically because I want it to be extremely rare, and having it appear on one of the most powerful models in the game suggests it's not going to be that common.

The other Space Marine datasheets in the WarCom article demonstrate some more welcome streamlining. The Sternguard Veterans now have one profile for their basic ranged weapons but three different fire modes, effectively a melta profile, plasma profile, and bolter profile.

This reflects the fact that there are clearly melta and plasma combi-weapons on the squad without posing any modelling challenges, while making the fixed loadout Sternguard from the Leviathan boxed set less frustrating to run - everyone has the same guns.

 

The Sternguard's combi-weapons do however lose Devastating Wounds, which seems to continue the pattern from Codex Orks of reducing this Ability's prevalence. Guilliman keeps Dev Wounds on the Emperor's Sword - which incidentally gets bumped up to S10, so it can still wound Marines on a 2+, and replaces four of its attacks with Cleave 2 so it doesn't become too effective as an anti-vehicle weapon - while the newly revealed Librarian also gets it on the Hazardous profile of his psychic attack.

Speaking of continuing trends from Codex Orks, so far the only Space Marines datasheet with Feel No Pain is Guilliman. That's a good thing. Thematic as it may be, it's a messy mechanic that wrecks dice rolling during attack resolution for multi-model units.

I'd be remiss not to give a shout out to the Terminator Squad here. We knew Toughness 6 and Strength 5 Storm Bolters were coming, but not that the Termies would get +1AP against targets within nine inches - making them far more effective at clearing their target on the turn they deep strike. Returning to the theme of quality-of-life improvements, the Cyclone Missile launcher now has a flat eight shots. Which might feel wrong if you're used to random shots on blast weapons, but you're still rolling to hit.

I'm impressed by what I've seen. The changes seem rational, thematic, and no more complicated than what we had in 10th edition. If this is the direction of travel for all the Warhammer 40k factions, then I'm on board. What do you think? Would love to hear your thoughts in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Historic mini maker Gripping Beast prepares to shut its doors after 30 years
content:
UK-based miniature maker Gripping Beast has announced plans to close its doors after 30 years making historical and fantasy miniatures. Its range of models, which includes over 6,000 miniatures the studio developed itself and two lines acquired from other companies, is now up for sale, with a buyer yet to be found.

Gripping Beast has been a stalwart in the UK historical miniature scene since it opened in 1996. Originally founded by brothers Colin and Duncan Patten, American readers are most likely to have encountered it via Saga, the historical and fantasy warband game, which it co-published with designers Studio Tomahawk, but it has a truly extensive line.

Writing on its website and social media on Friday, Gripping Beast states "we unfortunately aren't getting any younger, some of us are getting considerably creakier, and our small team has been reduced by recent retirements". As a result, the team has decided to wind down the business.

The owners state "we would very much like to see the business continue under new ownership", and "we would be delighted if someone came along and decided that they fancied taking on the rather enormous pile of miniatures we've spent decades creating and looking after".

Gripping Beast's output ranges include the eponymous 28mm Gripping Beast Miniatures, the modern combat MoFo range, Polemarch Successors, and The Woodbine Design Company, a specialist range for oddities and one-offs. In 2021 it acquired Front Rank Figurines and its varied 28mm historicals and 40mm American War of Independence miniatures; and last year it acquired the 15mm Lurkio Ancients and Renaissance ranges. These model lines are all up for sale with the business.

The studio has also manufactured several ranges that it doesn't also own, and has provided some information about their fate via Facebook. SAGA has already passed outside Gripping Beast's hands - distribution has already been taken on by North Star Military Figures, while Studio Tomahawk will continue to make and produce it. "The Ragnarok Fantasy range as well as Shieldwall Miniatures will return to Shieldwall Miniatures", while "the Ragnarok historical range will return to Colin Patten" and the "Calpe Miniatures range will return to Peter Fitzgerald".

In the short term, customers will still be able to place orders via the Gripping Beast website, and the studio says "we promise to fulfil all orders that come in". You'll also be able to meet the team at the conventions Partizan II and Warfare. But at some unspecified point, web sales will shut down to allow the team to process remaining orders and shutter the business.

If you've got a sturdy collection of Gripping Beast minis - or fond recollections of meeting the team at a show - come and share them in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: D&D head Dan Ayoub on listening and learning from the OGL: "We lost sight of what was important"
content:
It's been just over one year since Dan Ayoub became head of Dungeons and Dragons. For many reasons, 2025 was an interesting time to take over. Wizards of the Coast had just finished the rollout of D&D 5.5e. Yet the game's community was still reeling from a controversy now two years old: the OGL debacle. Trust was at an all time low when Ayoub became the face of the brand.

Since his promotion, rebuilding trust has been a top priority, and Ayoub tells me he's not done yet. He describes his first year in charge as a mix of "really rewarding" and "fucking terrifying". He shares the wins he's proud of, the lessons he's learned, and the hopes he has for D&D's future.

We trade stories of our home games; he's DMing a first-ever campaign for his 14-year-old son and friends, and it tells me a lot about his approach to shaping Dungeons and Dragons. Ayoub has talked in past press events about his 'holistic' approach to the brand, but the force driving his decisions is personal, individual. His strategy is intensely human, and his greatest achievement since becoming head of D&D? He thinks it's listening.

Wargamer: Just over a year ago, you took over as head of D&D, and you began with some bold promises. A brand-new franchise model, listening to community voices, and earning the trust of the community. Do you feel you've delivered on these promises so far?

Dan Ayoub: I like to think we have made great strides. Bluntly, we're recovering from a lot of missteps - very loud, very public missteps. And we're not going to fix it in one year. I can talk 'til the cows come home, but we've got to show more than tell, and that is going to take some time. I'm very conscious that it's going to take a lot of time to win back the trust to the extent that I would like. Having said that, I think we've started strongly, and a lot of these things are still happening behind the scenes.

The intent of the franchise model was to bring everything under one roof. Videogames don't sit over here and do very disparate things from TTRPG and entertainment. You're going to start seeing more of that come together in terms of listening.

Honestly, if I would give myself good grades on one thing in particular over the past year, I think it's been listening. We established the community council. I've personally spent a bunch of time talking to not just fans, but retailers and consumers.

And then, of course, there's the classic creators. On a personal note, as a fan, I was very personally frustrated by some of the breaks I had seen happen with the people who created what we're all enjoying today. I think we made great strides there.

I'll be honest with you, Mollie. I don't think I'll ever get to a point where I feel like 'okay, I don't need to do this any more'. I think this conversation always needs to be happening. I'm always going to want to be listening.

I love D&D, and the reason I took this job is because I want to get it back to how I remember it. I want people to share the types of stories you and I just shared, but there's a road to that. I'm very hard on myself, particularly where that stuff is concerned, and I don't think I'm ever going to be satisfied, but I will absolutely be holding myself to those promises I made at the beginning.

Repairing broken trust has been a theme in many of your discussions of D&D. That means we need to talk about the OGL. Where did Wizards go wrong, and what lessons has your team learned since?

D&D is about, for, and by the fans. That's the first fundamental point that we can never lose. I think, over the course of several years, we lost sight of what was important. We lost sight of who our audience was.

Another way the brand veered off course is making the mistaken assumption that there's a one-size-fits-all for D&D, which is absolutely not the case. It's certainly not my job to tell you how to play D&D. It is my job to give you the tools and fun experiences with which you can jump into it.

But I don't want to skirt the focus of your question. It was a rug pull, right? A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them. In some cases, it's caused damage we are still trying to fix today. So I understand the hesitancy of 'okay, here's this new guy saying all these things'.

My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break. I'm keenly aware it's going to take me a long time to repair this, but my hope is people will give the benefit of the doubt as we continue to show that lessons have been learned. This is a new direction, a new voice, and a new spirit and energy behind D&D.

Coming into a senior role after all this happened must have been quite a bit of pressure. This didn't just change how people view D&D and Wizards of the Coast; it had ripple effects on the entire industry. It changed the ecosystem.

It really did. I'm a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography. It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.

And it was a fucking terrifying decision point for me. I've been playing D&D my entire life, and I was very aware of the state of things when I was coming in. I love this thing so much. There was always that fear: 'God, I don't want to do anything to damage this thing I love so much'. But at the same time, I love this thing so much, and I can't bear to see it in this state.

I approached it from a place of love first and foremost. What do I want to see as a fan? What do I want? But I'm not going to lie, it was absolutely terrifying coming into it. I feel like we've made some great strides just in that year, but I don't think that journey ever stops.

The OGL has been on my mind ever since the Gen Con Keynote. A large part of that keynote announced outside creators would be working on D&D, from Icons to the new Ravenloft and Forgotten Realms books. I thought, after years of everyone being siloed and isolated thanks to the OGL, it was interesting how everyone was beginning to collaborate again. What inspired this move?

Honestly, it's the right thing to do for D&D. I don't want us to be the only voice for D&D, and part of the challenge for the brand is - let's be real - that's what happened. The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that's not how D&D grows.

I want to bring more people in to tell more stories. D&D means very different things to very different people. We can't tell all of the stories, and I'm certainly not arrogant enough to think there aren't brilliant storytellers all over the world. I want those voices.

What was rewarding for me was, when we laid out that we want to bring all these voices back, I was thrilled with the level of excitement from these partners. It was almost like this exhale of relief.

We're constantly having meetings with the partners we talked about [at the Keynote], but other partners as well. I look back on my own memories of when I thought D&D was at its greatest, it was when we had all these other voices. And I know not one voice works for everyone. We can't make every product we release be for everyone, but everyone should see something for themselves in our roadmap.

And the only way we can do that is bring on partners. We had a partner in the office today, just running through ideas, and it was honestly a bunch of shit we would not have thought of. Those kinds of voices energize the brand, and we're only stronger when our partners are with us.

It feels fitting considering that the product being made is a game that only functions when everyone works together.

Absolutely. There's almost an irony to it. The fundamental mantra is don't split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.

So now, how do we make sure that everyone is together, excited, and has a piece they can feel ownership over? That goes for classic creators, too. We reached out to Margaret [Weis] and Tracy [Hickman] and Luke [Gygax] and Bob [Salvatore], because these are fundamental voices. As I said at Gen Con, we stand on the shoulders of giants. Those folks, as we quickly learned, still have a lot of stories to tell.

Returning to D&D's past is exciting, but with so much focus on established designers, settings, and characters, how are you helping to shape D&D's future? How are you opening the door for new designers and new ideas while also celebrating what came before?

We're in early stages now. You're going to see us talk about a few other things over the course of the coming year. Don't take this literally, because it's a bad example I'm going to use, but I was a big fan of Dragon [Magazine] back in the day. Its modules were a great way to find new talent, mechanics, and systems.

I'm absolutely not launching a magazine or anything like that, but one of the things I always loved about D&D is how it found places for new creators to come in with new ideas. And, when they resonated, there was a way to amplify that so it could grow into something else. We need to and want to create those kinds of opportunities.

Then there's the question of how you make new fans as well. There are going to be multiple lines within D&D, and bringing new folks into it is a huge part of what I want to do. Someone is going to get to sit in this chair and celebrate D&D's 100-year anniversary, and that only happens if we continue to grow and bring new fans in.

We're doing things outside of the RPG. There's the recent Netflix announcement and the stuff we're doing with HBO. Obviously, Stranger Things has been a fantastic way to bring in new fans.

But, to use the Icons example, I want to make sure that throughout that, there is something for everybody. Whether you're curious and want to get in - and we'll be making announcements around that topic soonish - all the way up to someone that's been playing since 1974.

These aren't the only voices you've brought in. You've also created community advisory groups to bring more voices to the table. How has working with these groups gone?

It has been great. The candor has been fantastic. People are good about talking to us about where they feel we've gone off the rails in the past, and about what they don't want to see. But it's been a good mix of positive too.

In that first session, they gave us great feedback on the positive side of the seasons model, and I have huge thanks to them because their feedback was 'you're doing all these cool things, but you're doing a terrible job telling people about it'. It was actually after that debrief we said 'we need to publicize our roadmap, they're absolutely right.'

We've had product ideas that have gone away as a result. When there's weird things we want to try out, they're a great first point for us. It's hard to read the cereal box when you're on the inside, and having a layer of people who are extremely comfortable telling you 'you guys are fucking dumb, and here's why' is really helpful for us.

It's worked better than I could have hoped. It's certainly something we're going to continue. I would like to think of other types of setups we can do for more direct feedback. The advisory board's never going anywhere, but we've been playing with other models as well, because I don't want to lose that hands-on touch. It's something I value personally. It's why I go to shows myself - I love to hear from people directly.

That's it for our landmark D&D interview with Dan Ayoub - for now. What's your take? At this pivotal moment for D&D, what do you most want to see Dan and his team deliver? Come join the free Wargamer Discord community and let us know - there's sure to be some serious discussion on this one!

title: MTG Arena's Alchemy format is dead - here's what WotC should replace it with
content:
The digital only Magic: The Gathering format Alchemy is going to be cut from MTG Arena. Digitally-rebalanced cards will revert to their original wordings across all formats on September 22, while events and queues for Alchemy games will shut down on February 22 2027. Whether you're happy, sad, or - more likely - utterly ambivalent to see Alchemy go the way of the dodo, this could be a brilliant opportunity for the Arena team to bring other Magic formats to the platform to fill the void.

The final Alchemy set will be Alchemy: Reality Fracture, released on October 13. I hope that the game designers working on Alchemy-only cards have been rehomed into the teams who bring the ever-expanding range of paper MTG sets into Arena - but it would be excellent if they were trying one of these more ambitious projects instead!

Pauper

Pauper rules. This sixty card format's peculiar card pool - any and all cards that have ever been printed at common rarity, minus a banned list - gives the format surprising power yet also a feeling of being very fair. There are no real bombs, just great card combinations that span the entire history of the game. The result is that paper Pauper has the healthiest, most diverse metagame of any constructed format.

Getting parity with paper Pauper on Arena will take way longer than it did to import Pioneer. But a dedicated mode approximating Pauper would still be great. Arena already runs Midweek Magic events for common-only decks: give us a queue, events, incorporate the Pauper banlist and the cards that have been printed at common in paper and at higher rarirites on Arena, and we're off to the races.

Gladiator

Gladiator also rules - check out the Prof's video at the Tolarian Community College for a very quick rundown. This fan-supported Arena-only format uses 100 card singleton decks drawn from almost the entire Timeless pool, minus a banlist. Critically, there are no Commanders.

So while decks can play with broken powerful cards, but without the lynchpin Commander or the redundancy of running multiple copies of a card, players have to pull from far more of their card pool to support their strategies.

Gladiator has had very occasional Midweek Magic events, but it deserves its own queue. It also doesn't use rebalanced cards, so it's going to adapt to the loss of Alchemy very easily! As it stands, the best way to get involved is to join the Gladiator Discord community.

DanDȃn

DanDȃn rules so much. Rhystic Studies video 'Forgetful Fish', above, gives a great overview of how this fan format works and its history, but here's the basics. Both players play from a single deck, a blue pile of mischief cards - since there's only one library, manipulating it becomes a game within a game. The only source of damage is copies of DanDȃn, a 4/1 blue fish that can only attack an opponent who controls an island, and is sacrificed the moment you don't control one.

DanDȃn doesn't warrant its own queue, but it would make for a great recurring Midweek Magic event. Many variants to the original deck list exist that have surprisingly nuanced effects over the game, stopping it from getting old. And if nothing else, it's a hell of an education in how to play blue decks.

But what do you want to see? More effort to get true parity with paper Pioneer? Oathbreaker? Commander? Everyone says they want Commander, but a player roping out is going to waste three other players' time instead of one… Let us know your thoughts in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: This whimsical industrial board game lets you play a little mouse with big ambitions
content:
As much as I can respect the sheer mechanical graft at their core, I am often put off by the unrelenting seriousness of the likes of Brass Birmingham or Ticket to Ride. I prefer my industrialism with a side of whimsy, and it looks as though the folks at Skellig Games agree, at least as far as their latest board game project, Steam and Cheese, is concerned.

As described on the preview page for its upcoming crowdfunder, Steam and Cheese is a dice placement and resource management game where you take on the role of a mouse magnate aiming to dominate the cheese market. The game itself takes place in a cutesy alternative history where mice became the dominant species. Instead of oil barons and weapons manufacturers, this rodentine reality is full of cheese moguls and bewhiskered industrialists.

Over the course of a round, you'll be activating machines, managing your resources, and trying to wind up with as little wasted cheese or spoiled milk as possible - all while trying to prevent your opponents from doing the same. You'll use a tightly designed dice system to dictate which production machines you activate, while sending your adorable assistants to gather additional resources by zeppelin.

The crowdfunder itself is set to launch on September 15. What's more, Skellig Games seems confident in the quality of the product. Not only has the developer promised that a copy of the rulebook will be available for free for prospective backers to scrutinize, but there will also be a mod for virtual tabletop platform Tabletop Simulator which will allow players to try out Steam and Cheese for themselves.

Though I've not yet had a chance to play Steam and Cheese for myself, the numerous expository videos on the campaign preview page render me cautiously optimistic for the title's future. Should Steam and Cheese deliver, it may well find itself on our comprehensive list of the very best board games.

title: Games Workshop accidentally teases pleasingly nostalgic new Dwarf faction on web store
content:
In what was most likely a misstep from some poor soul in charge of the Warhammer Store's website, Games Workshop accidentally gave us a glimpse at an upcoming Dwarf faction for Age of Sigmar. While the Kharadron Overlords add a dynamic, steampunk-adjacent aesthetic to the game and the Fyreslayers are wonderfully reminiscent of Warhammer Fantasy's Dwarf Slayers, no Dwarfen offering from Age of Sigmar has really filled the void left by the more typical dwarfs of yesteryear. This is poised to change, thanks to the Khazalite Holds.

Games Workshop revealed several miniatures from the faction on the Warhammer Store, including some footsoldiers, some larger golem-like constructs, and what looks like a Dwarfen general. We've popped the image from the Warhammer Store banner below for your convenience. However, since Games Workshop has since taken down the webpage and has not provided high-res versions of the image, we'll all have to settle for a bit of blurriness in the meantime.

The dwarfen footsoldiers look stoic and unrelenting, their shields bearing traditional runes that fans of Warhammer Fantasy may well recognize. The golem looks stout as all hell, ready to deal out punishment with its greathammer - most likely as some sort of linebreaker. Last, and most impressive of all, we have the leader of the drawfen band. Wearing thick armour and remarkably well-plaited hair, our general sports a billowing cloak, great axe and a fetching headpiece (as well as a tactical rock for good measure).

Notably, aside from briefly posting the above image on the web store, Games Workshop has not released any further concrete information about the Age of Sigmar faction or the leak at the time of writing. We advise staying vigilant for rumours and hearsay. That said, it's very refreshing to see Age of Sigmar's dwarfs return to their aesthetic and thematic roots.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: CMON Faces Make-or-Break Moment as It Warns of “Prolonged Structural Downturn”
content:
CMON has issued a stark warning about its future, telling investors its core business is stuck in a “prolonged structural downturn” and still burning through more cash than it brings in. The tabletop crowdfunding giant is now racing to raise up to $17.5m from outside investors.

The warning landed alongside CMON’s H1 financial report, and it caps off a brutal 18 months for one of the biggest names in crowdfunded board games.

Parts of this article is based on info from BoardGameWire.

A Company Half Its Former Size

CMON has spent the past year and a half trying to stop the bleeding. The publisher has:

  • Cut its workforce in half
  • Sold off major IP including Zombicide, Blood Rage, and Cthulhu: Death May Die
  • Shut down its Singapore office
  • Halted new crowdfunding campaigns

Those moves have helped — but not enough to fix the underlying problem.

Losses Shrinking, But Cash Still Draining

The good news: CMON’s losses are shrinking fast.

The company posted a loss of just over $2m in the first half of 2026, compared to nearly $7m during the same stretch last year. Revenue also crept up more than 7% year-on-year, hitting $3.68m. Selling and distribution costs were cut by more than half, and administrative expenses dropped from $4.37m to $2.37m.

The bad news: it’s still not enough to keep the lights on without outside help.

CMON’s cash reserves have been in freefall. They sat at $3.9m at the end of 2022, fell to $2.1m by the end of 2024, and slipped to just over $900,000 by June 2025. In early August, the company revealed it had roughly $368,000 on hand — less than a month’s worth of operating expenses.

The Backer Problem: $14m in Undelivered Games

A huge chunk of CMON’s financial pressure comes down to games that backers have already paid for but haven’t received.

Eight crowdfunded titles remain undelivered, representing $14m raised from backers. The two biggest are **DC Super Heroes United** (over $4.4m raised) and DCeased (over $2.5m). Both were originally due last year, but have been delayed repeatedly and are now slated for Q1 2027.

CMON hasn’t completed fulfillment on a crowdfunding project since Zombicide: White Death in mid-2025. It has managed to ship some pre-orders — Cthulhu: Dark Providence, Marvel United: Witching Hour, and Dune: Desert War all went out in the first half of this year — but four more pre-order titles remain in limbo, including the Assassin’s Creed Role Playing Game.

The $17.5m Gamble

To stay afloat, CMON is leaning on a massive rights issue designed to raise up to HK$150.5m (about $19m). The plan lets existing shareholders buy three new shares for every one they already own.

There’s just one problem: shareholders barely took the bait. Only 7.76% of the new shares were claimed by the August deadline, leaving CMON scrambling to find more than $17.5m from other investors — a figure approaching 2.5-times the company’s entire valuation from its last share sale in February.

If the money comes through, here’s how CMON plans to spend it:

  • 40% — Day-to-day operations for roughly a year, including staff, royalties, shipping, and distribution
  • 20% — Paying down debts, including $2.46m owed to a company director and $385,000 in unsecured employee advances
  • 25% — Expansion into existing and new markets, with a focus on Europe, Japan, and the Philippines
  • 15% — Potential acquisitions in digital gaming

The final result of the rights issue is due September 15.

A Digital Pivot — With a Catch

That 15% digital acquisition budget is notable, especially since CMON just walked away from a planned $2.1m investment in NFT game maker Blissful Link. That deal would have valued Blissful Link at over $95m — despite the company posting a loss of about $197,000 in 2024 on revenues of just over $408,000.

CMON says it’s now hunting for one to three businesses, mostly in Asia-Pacific, valued between $1.3m and $2.5m each, to help build digital adaptations and companion apps. The publisher insists physical tabletop games remain its core business and that digital is meant to complement, not replace, them.

Where the Money Comes From Now

The report also lays bare just how dramatically CMON’s geographic revenue has shifted.

North America generated over $8.6m in the first half of 2021 — 57% of the company’s roughly $15.1m revenue at the time. By the first half of 2026, North and South America combined brought in just $642,000.

Europe has collapsed similarly, falling from about $4.5m to $982,000 over the same period.

Asia is now CMON’s largest market by a wide margin, generating over $2m and accounting for about 55% of total revenue — up from less than 10% in 2021. That’s not because Asia is growing, though. Revenue there is down roughly 37% since 2022. It’s just fallen far less than everywhere else.

What’s Next for Crowdfunding?

CMON said back in March that it intended to resume crowdfunding in the second half of 2026. Its latest report doesn’t repeat that promise. Instead, the company says new titles will be developed and launched “selectively” based on market conditions, available cash, and project readiness.

For a publisher built on the crowdfunding model, that’s a notable shift in tone — and a sign that CMON’s road back to stability is still a long one.

title: This Monty Python-esque comedy RPG lets you improv as a band of incompetent and dangerously powerful wizards
content:
Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is a new tabletop roleplaying game that allows players to become powerful and incompetent spellcasters.

The upcoming roleplaying game sees any number of players collaborating together to tell a story about a band of chaotic wizards. Similarly to the likes of absurdist, fantastical comedy such as the works of iconic British group Monty Python, alongside the likes of The Mighty Boosh and What We Do in the Shadows, Hello Wizard I have a Problem is all about rapid scenes infused by the strange and unexpected.

Unlike many other tabletop RPGs, Hello Wizard sees its players taking turns to take on the roles of player character and games master. Each scene in Hello Wizard has a single player take the spotlight as their spellcaster, with the goal of impressing their fellow sorcerers with their magic. The active player describes what spells their wizard casts, with the other players acting collectively as a GM and deciding how these spells can go wrong.

Players will use a Problem Generator included in the fantasy RPG’s rulebook as inspiration for what could go wrong with the wizards’ spells, with the book capable of making over “200,000” prompts for possible disastrous outcomes. Once every player has had the opportunity to step into the spellcasting spotlight at least a few times, the game ends and players tally up their ‘points’ - which are decided by a loose improv system - and determine who is the most impressive wizard.

The rules system for Hello Wizard is very straightforward and intended to be easy for players to learn. Setup for the tabletop RPG is also designed to be quick and easy, with players expected to start in little time. The rulebook for the game will contain advice and optional rules players can use to augment their playthroughs too.

Hello Wizard I have a Problem was created by Sam Armstrong, a tabletop RPG designer who has previously made titles such as All Bastard - a fantasy TRPG in which players take the roles of either a band of bragging heroes or the bastards they defeated - and horror roleplaying game Slasher. The artwork for the game was created by illustrator Evlyn Moreau, who has previously worked on RPGs like Liminal High School.

The crowdfunding campaign for Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is on Kickstarter until later this afternoon, with the title potentially being made available on Armstrong’s Itch.io page. A pledge of £8 ($10) will get backers a physical copy of the game in June, alternatively a PDF version is available for £4 ($5).

title: Re-enact Greta Gerwig’s Little Women with this coming-of-age tabletop RPG
content:
New tabletop roleplaying game, Castles in the Air, will enable players to re-enact their favourite coming-of-age stories.

Castles in the Air was inspired by the likes of classic coming-of-age period dramas such as Little Women by Louisa May Alcott - which was adapted into a 2019 film directed by Greta Gerwig and starring Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Laura Dern and Timothee Chalamet - and Anne of Green Gables by Lucy Maud Montgomery, which was adapted into a televisions series in 2017 by Netflix.

The upcoming roleplaying game will see players’ characters grow up together from children to adults during the historical era known as the Gilded Age, which took place in the USA from the 1870s to the 1890s and saw an increase in industrialisation, economic growth and migration to the US. Castles in the Air is a collaborative storytelling game in which players construct narratives that centre around the wonders and fears of childhood, before tackling the joys and hardships of adulthood.

Players begin the tabletop RPG as a tight-knit group of children, all of whom have great expectations of their futures and much quieter current lives. In this phase of the story, players develop a shared childhood together by doing the things rural and financially supported kids did during that era: like playing in their local farmlands, swimming in the lakes and watching the stars.

As the player characters grow up, they’ll begin exploring other feelings and ideas that come with age. Characters in the group might develop a crush on someone or form a heated rivalry with one of the other local children. All the while, the player group will grow up together, before eventually reaching adulthood and potentially finding themselves drifting apart as life takes them in different directions - perhaps to only meet once again.

Players will be able to create their characters in Castles in the Air by choosing from a variety of character roles inspired by classic archetypes, such as the troublesome scamp, studious bookworm or spoiled princess. Add onto this a dream, childhood relationships, a family background and a bosom enemy, and players can even create their favourite characters from the likes of Little Women or Anne of Green Gables.

Castles in the Air was designed and written by Melia Carraway, with contributions from co-created by the co-founders of the RPG’s publisher, Storybrewer’s Roleplaying, Vee Hendro and Hayley Gordon, who also co-designed Good Society: a tabletop RPG inspired by the works of Jane Austen.

The crowdfunding campaign for Castles in the Air is on Kickstarter until June 9th, with a pledge of AU$ 99 (£52/$77) getting backers a physical copy of the game in March 2025. Alternatively, players can get a digital version for a pledge of AU$ 34 (£18/$26).

title: Freak War throws Exploding Kittens and Pokémon into a blender for a trading card game you can play at parties
content:
Take the evolving monsters of Pokémon, cross them with the fast-playing chaos of party game hit Exploding Kittens and you end up with something that looks a lot like Freak War, a new party-game TCG that wants to offer the fun battles of trading card games without the effort of learning lots of rules or building a deck.

Freak War is the creation of Nate Galbraith, aka cartoonist sketchnate, who was inspired after watching kids trying to have Pokémon battles using Uno cards, before suggesting they play classic playing card game War (which you might also know as Battle) instead. The result was a mixture of all three, with Galbraith adding a collection of strange creatures to the cards.

Unlike the head-to-head battles of Pokémon, Freak War can be played with up to four (or more) players, who can simply split the shuffled deck between them to play - though there is the option to build your own custom decks if you really want to.

Everyone plays a creature at the same time, with the highest attack level winning the battle. Like Exploding Kittens, the many cards can also introduce various effects that shake things up, including the power to evolve into bigger creatures - Pokémon-style - and equip modifiers to your own or opponent’s cards to boost or reduce their strength.

Whether the players choose a card from their hand or simply flip the top of their deck depends on the mode they’re playing: the more chaotic War, or the more strategic Battle. Both modes can be modified further by King of the Hill and team rules.

If two players draw in attack level, they both discard a card before facing off by playing another creature. The overall winner takes all the cards played and adds them to their win pile, which are reshuffled into the player’s deck - the person who manages to claim all the cards from their opponents, wins.

The weird and wonderful creatures on the cards have a bit of lore behind them, having been created by the emergence of a second sun that mutated familiar animals like rabbits, foxes and fish into muscly fishpeople, a time-travelling tiger, a partying platypus, a dog with a goldfish bowl for a head, a sad bee and a Man Cat that appears to basically be a bloke in a cat costume, among others.

Modifier cards, meanwhile, range from a Super Sword (and a Super Duper Sword) to the power to swap cards with a rival, cancel a modifier or flip coins for the chance of a power boost. Some of the creature effects get playfully meta in the way you’d expect for a party game too, with the scrap-loving Fly Guy gaining power if there’s uneaten food near the players.

As someone who is admittedly tired of many copy-paste or just downright gross party games (looking at you, double-offending Cards Against Humanity clones), I’m fairly charmed by Galbraith’s goofy creations and the sprinkling of chaotic take-that gameplay in the form of a TCG. (The card layout is quite explicitly inspired by Pokémon cards.) Sure, it’s not going to be for everyone, but as something knowingly silly to fill five minutes with friends and family (especially younger players), it looks like solid, breezy fun for $20 a deck. With a bunch of different packs filled with dozens more creatures from buff penguins to cute-looking snails, I’m pretty intrigued just to see Galbraith’s interpretation of the nonsense of modern Pokémon evolutions, too.

Freak War has already passed its fairly modest crowdfunding goal of $10,000 over on Kickstarter, where its campaign will run until June 13th. The game itself is expected to land with backers next June, just in time to take on holiday.

title: New Blade Runner RPG expansion asks how far you’d go for the Replicant Rebellion
content:
A new expansion for the official Blade Runner tabletop roleplaying game invites you to join the Replicant Rebellion.

Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game is based on the series of films based on Phillip K Dick’s sci-fi novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep.

Blade Runner, the first of these films, was released in 1982 and directed by Ridley Scott. The film sees Harrison Ford play Deckard, a Blade Runner - an officer whose sole purpose is to hunt and eliminate Replicants, or human-looking androids - who is tasked with finding and killing three escaped Replicants. Following on from the original film, Blade Runner 2049 is a sequel directed by Denis Villeneuve and starring Ryan Gosling. In Blade Runner 2049, Gosling stars as K, a Replicant Blade Runner who must follow the trail of a long-escaped Replicant fugitive and investigate the truth behind her death.

Both films take place in the same fictional science fiction universe wherein Replicants were designed and created entirely to fulfil the needs and wants of their human makers. The Blade Runner franchise is known for its cyberpunk aesthetics, as well as grim view of a near-future wherein corporations are able to commit terrible acts without consequence and exploit large swathes of people.

Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game usually has players taking the roles of Blade Runners within the LA police department during the time period between the first and second films. However, rather than fulfilling their duties as Replicant hunting officers, the next expansion for the sci-fi RPG sees players abandoning their post to join the Replicant Underground.

Replicant Rebellion is a new expansion for the Blade Runner RPG that sees players get recruited into the Replicant Underground, a secret organisation whose goal is to ensure the freedom and liberation of Replicants: whatever the cost.

Players will see themselves become members of the movement - running their own independent crew as they carry out a variety of missions on behalf of the Underground. From laying charges for explosives, sabotaging the Replicant trade and smoking out moles, players must be prepared for all manner of tasks. Members of the group might even find themselves stuck between a rock and a hard place, as they balance their personal morality with the operations of the Replicant Underground.

Both the Replicant Rebellion expansion and the Blade Runner roleplaying game were published and created by Free League Publishing, the studio behind other licensed TRPGs such as the Alien Roleplaying Game.

A crowdfunding campaign for Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game - Replicant Rebellion will be launched on Kickstarter on May 28th.
